#4055. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4053. Exclusive – Behind The Romance: Rockstar Talks GTAVI’s Jason And Lucia

After dozens of hours exploring Leonida, I have a lot of positive things to say about Grand Theft Auto VI, and shared as much in our review of the game. But for my part, the feature that elevated the game most prominently above Rockstar Games’ other (excellent) games wasn’t its graphics, missions, or action – it was the storytelling and interplay between the two lead protagonists. Jason and Lucia bring heart, emotional depth, and a sense of genuine threat to the crime fantasy, as you grow attached to them and start cheering for them against all the odds stacked against them.

We reached out to senior members of the Rockstar Games team to ask about their thoughts on Jason and Lucia, and this is what they had to share.

During my playthrough, the Jason and Lucia dynamic really elevated the experience, adding heart and emotional weight to the expected mix of action, driving, and activities around Leonida. Was a couple or romantic relationship the plan or goal for the game from very early on in development, or did that come later? Do you see the focus on Jason and Lucia’s relationship as one of the features that separates Grand Theft Auto VI from your prior work on storytelling in the game series?

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design: “The dual protagonists and the relationship between the two of them was there from very early in development, but exactly how that was expressed in the game did change over time. It was an enormous challenge for us to get them working together in the open world together and finding exactly how that would work. As we started to layer in more mechanics, dialogue, and incremental features across all teams, it just clicked at some point. The ability to be together in the open world also allowed us for new ways to tell the story of the game and to bring some of the exposition and narrative into the open world in a way we hadn’t been able to do before. Hearing these little bits of dialogue as you are just tooling around the world that have specific context to what you as a player have just been doing in the story really knits it all together.”

The player has a choice for how to develop the relationship between the two leads, but I imagine most players are drawn toward helping it thrive. In early playtests, is that what you observed?

Katie Pica, Design Director: Player Systems & Progression:“Overall, we’ve seen that players are invested in supporting Jason and Lucia’s relationship but we don’t favor a specific path through the game, it is completely down to player choice.”

It feels like a lot of the game’s driving narrative beats factor for a close connection between Jason and Lucia. Was it challenging to craft variations that included a more tense or distant connection between the two? Is that even possible?

Luke Howard, Senior Design Director: Missions & Visualization:“One of the core goals of this game was to tell the story of Jason and Lucia with a base line relationship where they are amicable, if just platonic, as they still share the same ultimate goals and need each other to achieve them. So, this gave us a good platform on the main flow to expand particularly intense or emotional moments they experience with variation that can expand on their romantic relationship, while not losing anything if that doesn’t exist. In short, we did develop variation in scenes and interactions that range from subtle to more significant, but done in a way that should feel authentic to the player’s choices, relationship-wise and also criminal profile.

One example is after Lucia helps Kordell’s gang pull off an intense armored truck robbery she shares the information with Raul’s crew. Afterwards Jason pulls Lucia aside to see how she's coping. This moment carries several variations where the performance direction was captured multiple ways to cover a range emotional energy between them. The actors deliveries are brilliant and nuanced – these small tender moments are where we tried to craft pieces that when added up together over the course of the story, author an authentic version of the player’s Jason and Lucia.”

Were there any fictional couples or real-life couples that the team looked at for inspiration in shaping the Jason and Lucia dynamic, whether those couples came from big crime stories or not?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“We definitely started by looking at all the “couple on the run” movies. There are a lot of them but the ones that we kept coming back to were Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway in Bonnie and Clyde, McQueen and MacGraw in The Getaway (the Jim Thomson book is also great), True Romance, Thelma and Louise. Clooney and JLo’s dynamic in Out of Sight, as well. And then a lot of buddy movies actually – Riggs and Murtaugh, Butch and Sundance, Mike Lowry and Marcus Burnett, etc. for their back and forth together. In terms of having a game where the characters can change based on how you play and whether you really lean into and enjoy the crime spree we thought about how both Pulp Fiction and Natural Born Killers start with a couple in a diner pulling out guns, but then how different those couples are and how different those scenarios play out. Jason and Lucia are a lot tougher than Tim Roth and Amanda Plummer but we liked the idea of telling a story where Jason and Lucia could end up being closer to either end of that spectrum based on what the player was doing.”

Sex and intimacy are notoriously complicated and challenging to present in games. How did you aim to strike a balance with their private moments together that felt authentic? Any thoughts about how or why it’s so challenging to present adult relationships in video games?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“This is definitely something we thought a lot about and spent a long time trying to get right. The actors who play Jason and Lucia were so good, and they had a natural chemistry and part of it was just trying to capture some of that.

There’s this trade off in making games between player control and then scripted scenarios. We try and give the player as much control as we can because we are working in an interactive medium and actually doing something rather than watching it is going to feel more powerful. But then you have the ability to really mess around and break the illusion of a tender or romantic moment or whatever it is. So the relationship aspect of this story is there if a player wants to engage in it, but if they don’t the story can play out differently.”

In its best moments of genuine support, regular connection, open communication, and flirty or engagement with one another, Jason and Lucia can come across as a pretty ideal model of good relationships – even while they’re simultaneously committing major crimes together. Was that juxtaposition of a healthy romantic relationship against an external world of illicit activity an explicit goal for how the narrative came together?

Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative:“That was the goal, yes. You are really living with these characters – they’re eating, sleeping, showering, throwing away their trash, or not. The relationship needed to feel real to sit alongside all of that. Then even just as a development team, we live with these characters for years and years. We wanted them to be people we could like, care about, and root for. And they needed to like each other. But then the world itself is so crazy and chaotic and seemingly on the brink of collapse.

When we set out to make this game, and go into that multiyear development marathon, we said we wanted to spend our time working on something with heart, and with some characters you could care about and root for. It’s barely worth even stating, but we are living in a time when people are divided along almost every line, and feelings about the future are pretty bleak. We wanted to create a world that held up a mirror to that, showed that fever pitch of craziness that we are all maybe a couple of bad decisions away from, but we wanted the story we were going to tell to have something positive at its core and the message that human connection is better than division.”

The game automatically moves you to play one character or another at certain points, but for many sequences, you can choose your playable lead. In your experience playing and watching others play, do most players gravitate toward one character or another as “their character?”

Stephen Donkin, Vice President of Design:“It really varied in our playthroughs. They are both such great characters and performances that people seemed to gravitate to both of them in different ways. But overall, we have found the split of time between characters to be relatively even on a per-playthrough and also at a macro level.”

#4052. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4051. GTA 6's Physical Launch Has Been An Astronomical Success, Despite No Discs

All eyes have been on the launch of GTA 6 this month, with the game's so-called physical launch being a particularly interesting litmus test for the future of the industry.

It turns out that even without any discs, GTA 6 has proven to be a monumental success in terms of physical sales. This comes via Christopher Dring at The Game Business, who states that the game enjoyed the largest physical launch since 2019 in the UK, generating £32 million in revenue in just three days.

He goes on to state that GTA 6 is the "No.17 biggest physical game launch in the UK since records began in 1995".

In France, it's estimated that over 1 million physical copies were sold in the first three days, a figure that Dring states is comparable to GTA 5 back in 2013. In Spain, meanwhile, the game achieved the largest physical launch in the chart's history.

It's safe to say then that this has comfortably dwarfed pretty much anything that Nintendo has put out in recent years. Normally of course, we'd be celebrating such success – even if the game isn't actually available on Nintendo systems – but the fact that it's a code-in-a-box release raises a few eyebrows.

With GTA 6 being such a success, Sony will no doubt view this as validation that it made the right decision in ceasing the production of discs from 2028. Other large companies will also likely see it as proof that customers don't care about discs anymore, and will likely lean toward download codes much sooner than Sony's cut-off date.

Nintendo itself, meanwhile, probably won't do anything different – at least for the time being. Stats from recent financial reports indicate that Switch and Switch 2 players still value cartridges, with physical sales still making up close to half of the company's total first-party sales.

Still, it's a troubling result for folks who are still all-in on physical games. It certainly indicates that while there are plenty of folks who begrudge Sony's decision to stop the production of discs, there are many, many more people who just don't give a hoot.

#4049. Why Do I Want To Paint The Walls In Grand Theft Auto VI?

I admire the cozy sim genre. Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own. In an odd way, I find the genre stressful, arguably the opposite of its intended purpose. I will happily and cathartically guide Grace Ashcroft through the tense hallways of Rhodes Hill in Resident Evil Requiem, but Pokémon Pokopia’s seemingly endless list of to-dos makes me sweat. It’s just not my genre, and I have come to terms with that.

Grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics. Bird (and animal) watching, for example, is apparent and encouraged early in the experience. You can also fix up your somewhat dilapidated home from almost the moment you are let loose outside of the opening tutorial missions.

And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.

I climbed to the roof to fix the leak and replaced all the stairs leading up to the home before I ever participated in the game’s namesake and stole a car. Normally, it’s the kind of interaction I skip or choose not to engage with, given the option. Or, I do the bare minimum to progress. Sure, I have all the options in the world to build and decorate a house and make it my own, but… that feels like a lot of work. And I am not an artist.

The “cozy” elements of Grand Theft Auto VI are admittedly different from those in a game like Pokopia or Animal Crossing. You’re not designing your home (though you can pick a paint color), but it feels similar, and I am trying to figure out why I enjoy it here as opposed to other games. Is it because Jason and Lucia are so instantly believable as human beings that I want their home to be nicer?

After some thought, I think it might just come down to Grand Theft Auto VI’s consistently impressive visual fidelity. Replacing the shingles on the roof, for example, offers a close-up look at Jason’s character model, and you can practically feel the texture of the asphalt while the heat of the sun beats down.

I don’t have confirmation, but it also just feels like someone at Rockstar did exhaustive research on what the process of replacing a roof shingle should look like, even if, I’m sure, it probably doesn’t quite work that way in the real world. Jason makes it look incredibly easy, to the point that it had me questioning if I should be climbing up to my own roof and taking care of some loose shingles myself. And you know what is a lot of fun? Watching someone who is good at something do the thing they’re good at.

I’m now into the driving and shooting part of the game (and enjoying that, too!), but I am shocked at how grateful I was to have the option to stay home and put up drywall.

#4048. Feature: Seven Improvements We'd Still Love To See In GTA 6

There's no two ways about it: GTA VI is a blummin' brilliant game, well worthy of its universally acclaimed 99 Metacritic score. But just because we gave it a 10/10 here at Pure Xbox doesn't mean there isn't still some wiggle room for improvement.

Both Fraser and I have put many hours into this enormous RPG already, and have come away floored by its grandeur. However, we've also noticed a few things we'd like to see fixed or added to GTA VI to make it even better. Think of this article like adding marshmallows to a hot chocolate: we're looking to take something great and make it even sweeter.

We've whipped up a few of our own suggestions and mixed in some from across the world wide webbies to bring you our top improvements we'd like to see in GTA VI. Let's get into it:

On this page: Seven Improvements We'd Still Love To See In GTA 6

You've all noticed the darkness that appears from time to time around the screen, right? That's a vignette and GTA VI is a big fan of them. It's most noticeable when you're booking it down the North 97 highway or, in the worst-case scenario, flying over the Keys as shown in the above screenshot.

GTA VI uses vignettes to cleverly draw your focus to the most important parts of the screen. I honestly think it's a great technique for making things feel more cinematic. Although, it is quite pants that there's no option to reduce its intensity or turn it off altogether. If Rockstar could give us the ability to toggle the vignette on and off, that would be great, because it also seems to be one of the most requested changes amongst GTA VI players.

Something I've grown increasingly aware of is the inability to wait or sleep to pass time across Leonida. I was particularly irked after an 18-hole crazy golf competition against Jason saw the sun set on us, and I didn't fancy driving all the way back to my lodging in Vice City. I wanted to pass time in my car or a nearby eatery, but my only option appeared to be the 4-5 minute drive home - made worse knowing that once morning hit, I'd just want to do the drive back and play golf in the daylight.

It's probably the fault of Red Dead Redemption 2 and its extremely handy wilderness camps. They were great in a pinch to let you pass time quickly. What would be great is if GTA VI gave players the option to rough it in their car for the night or find a nearby hotel room or something.

I was on a mission to pick up some prescription drugs when my car was escorted slowly into an enemy compound and the camera suddenly switched from third-person to first-person. Seeing Lucia's impeccable nails gripped around the steering wheel made me realise there's no legitimate way to drive from a behind-the-wheel perspective.

Sure, there's that glitch that lets you play GTA VI in first-person, but it would be better if Rockstar implemented an additional first-person POV for driving.

It seems like a bit of a no-brainer, but we'd love to see AMD FSR 4.1 implementation on Xbox Series X. GTA VI is already up-and-running with FSR 4.1 on Xbox Series S which brings internal resolutions up from 720p to 1080p output. It's good going on XSS, but we'd like to see what it can do with XSX.

If a game launches with a good Photo Mode, then you may as well tack an extra 10 hours onto my playthrough. But GTA VI? Maybe add another 20-30 hours. It's gorgeous!

The Photo Mode in this game is already solid. You can set up light sources, adjust focus and aperture, and as a graduate photographer, I think it's all rather intuitive. There's even a selfie mode where players can pose Jason and Lucia together, adjust their facial expressions and change their poses.

What I'd like to see is that same flexibility expand beyond selfie mode. I'd like to be able to adjust the lovers to better match the photos I'm trying to create. It was during a tense getaway, four-stars and neck-deep in trouble, that I thought I'd take an action shot, only to find Jason had blinked and Lucia looked bored as hell. It would be great to have the option to adjust expressions, head directions, poses and all that sort of stuff.

Please fix the sliders when handling amounts of money, Rockstar. Please. It's not the biggest fix, nor the most elaborate, so I'll keep it brief.

Whenever I open my phone to buck myself some cash, I often struggle to select the right amount quickly. It takes too long for the slider to speed up as I increase the amount, but then it very quickly gets out of control, and I end up overshooting my intended figure. Plus, the sound it makes is quite horrid.

What would help is having set increments to scroll through, say, $1, $10, $50, $100 and so on. It might just smooth out the experience a smidge.

I'd like to wrap up with a quickfire segment of some of our own suggestions on how Rockstar could improve GTA VI, but also some of yours. So, let's get through it.

I'd love to be able to call NPC buddies like Cal for a round of crazy golf. At the moment, playing with a partner is limited to Jason and Lucia. I'm all for love, but sometimes you need some friendly bonding too.

Another one I'd personally like to see is custom music stations on in-game radios. Now, I know this isn't something likely to happen, but it would be cool to link my Spotify and Rockstar accounts to play my own curated playlists.

Oh, and for the love of all things matrimony, please let me make a coffee for Jason/Lucia and actually give it to them. I've experienced Jason asking for a cuppa joe, so let me do the do, y'know?

Something Fraser mentioned he'd like to see is additional minigames like bowling or darts added to the game. The developers said they ran out of time for things like this, so maybe they could add them as a post-launch update.

And to wrap up, I've spotted folks online requesting the ability to dial any phone number like you could in previous games, as well as blind firing around cover during firefights, buying housing property, and having save states pick up directly where you left off.

So, there you have it. Some of our suggestions and some we've found out in the wild, but we'd love to hear your ideas on what might make GTA VI a better game. Be sure to chat with us in the comments!

#4047. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4046. 10 Best Anime Games That'll Get You Into The Series

Ben Veress is a Contributing Features Writer based in Melbourne and has spent over five years covering gaming news and media.

I think it's fair to say anime can be tough to break into. As someone who started One Piece recently, I can feel the color drain from my face whenever I take a look at the episode count and realise I've barely scraped the surface of what's to come. Not to mention the abundance of filler episodes stretching the series out longer than Luffy in Gear 5.

Which is why, in my humble opinion, games have been an underrated way to onboard people into certain franchises. Oftentimes, you get your standard arena fighters, which are more than happy to dump an entire roster of characters into a game and call it a day. However, some games go the extra mile and retell entire arcs from the series, depicting some of the biggest moments and letting you play out those major fights.

This list discusses the best Anime-inspired action games that capture the genre far better than SAO: Echoes of Aincrad.

As someone who's played their fair share of anime games as a stand-in for watching the series, only to later become a full-fledged fan of the show, I'm a fervent believer in the pipeline.

That's why today we'll look at the 10 best anime games that can bring you into the series if 200+ episodes feels a bit too daunting to start with.

Saint Seiya is one of those series I always heard about, yet always put off watching for whatever reason. The series has a strong reputation in Japan and is arguably one of the most successful shounen anime of all time. Still, it can feel a bit tough jumping on the bandwagon, which is where Soldier's Soul comes in. Its Legend of Cosmo mode runs from the Twelve Houses of the Sanctuary through the Hades arc, with the anime-only Asgard arc slotted in too.

Like a few other games on this list, this is a fairly standard 3D arena fighter, so it's not the most balanced for a competitive environment. That said, its retelling of the anime's story captures what fans love about the series. The game's Legend of Cosmo mode runs from the Twelve Houses of the Sanctuary to the Hades arc. It also includes the anime-only Asgard arc for some extra content.

It can throw you in at the deep end, since it skips a fleshed-out introduction to Seiya and his companions, but it doesn't take long to pick up the group's dynamic and what makes them stand out.

Fist of the North Star is one of the great cult classics of 80s anime, and Ken's Rage 2 is a wonderful retelling of its best moments, and then some. In its Legend Mode, the game follows the entire manga, starting with a reworked take on the Raoh saga and pushing through the Celestial Emperor and Land of Shura arcs. For long-term fans of the series, it also includes a "Dream Mode", which works as some fun "What If" scenarios if you're hungry for more story.

The game plays out pretty similarly to Dynasty Warriors, and you'll find yourself mowing down hordes of nameless foes. Except instead of using swords and spears, in Fist of the North Star, you use your fists, which can lead to some pretty fun head-popping interactions in the game.

This might not land for some, as, granted, the legions of mohawked raiders do make you yearn for some variety here and there. That said, the game nails several of those big boss fight moments that make the downtime between the battles solid build-up. The hordes of mohawked raiders do blur together after a while, but the moments that made the series iconic still land. Dream Mode adds original stories for side characters too, though Legend Mode is where newcomers should start.

Not all great anime games have to be your standard 3D arena fighter that closely follows the anime (as great as those are). Sometimes they can be a fun arcade soccer game that gives any FIFA game a run for its money. Captain Tsubasa is a fairly nostalgic anime, but was brought back for a run in 2018, which this game follows.

Its Episode: Tsubasa mode follows Nankatsu Middle School through the entire National Middle School Tournament from the 2018 anime, complete with the famous matches and wildly over-the-top special shots.

That said, because the game hits the ground running, we don't get a lot of time to learn about Tsubasa's backstory and his rivalry with Kojiro Hyuga and Jun Misugi. A neat benefit of the game's storytelling is that the story can shift away from canon depending on how your matches play out. Personally, I think these are neat and make diving into the series more exciting, seeing what changed and how certain characters are fleshed out more.

Plus it's a great arcade soccer game in its own right, so even if you're not too invested in the story, you have some pretty engaging gameplay at the least.

It's crazy to think about how long JoJo's Bizarre Adventure has been around. Long before the series would launch into the mainstream thanks to its meme status, Capcom turned Part 3 into the gorgeous 2D fighter Heritage for Future for the PlayStation 1 and the Sega Dreamcast. This retro entry follows Jotaro Kujo and the Joestar group on their trek to Egypt to take down DIO, and the PS1 version's Super Story Mode goes further by retelling the arc with a few extra fights and minigames.

I don't think I'm ruffling any feathers when I say that the Stardust Crusaders arc is one of the most important arcs in the entire series. That is mostly due to its introduction of Stands, the power system the series is famously known for. That, and it's the first definitive arc where the JoJo franchise really comes into its own, and the video game helps capture that spirit. Capcom's sprite work also stays faithful to Hirohiko Araki's art, letting every fighter feel as strange and specific as the Stand they're built around.

Sadly, both the PS3 and Xbox versions were delisted in 2014. So, unless you grabbed it at the time (or are open to less-than-conventional methods of obtaining the game), you're stuck with the classic retro versions.

Koei Tecmo is now the undisputed goats of adapting anime into video games, and it wouldn't have that reputation without the first Attack on Titan game. Released as A.O.T.: Wings of Freedom in Europe, the game retells the events of the first game, letting you play through the fall of Wall Maria right through to the Survey Corps hunt for the Female Titan. There's also a fair few side missions that help fill the gap between those big story beats so you're not left too much out of the loop.

Of course, it wouldn't be an Attack on Titan game with the ODM gear, and I'm happy to say that the game nails the power fantasy of zipping through the air to cut a Titan's neck. Even better, it doesn't give you awful motion sickness like when other games or mods attempt to recreate a similar playstyle.

This is DualShockers' preview of Attack on Titan 3, the penultimate entry in the AOT Video Game series developed by Omega Force and published by Koei Tecmo.

I'm speaking anecdotally here, as my lifelong obsession with Bleach entirely stemmed from this game appearing on a pre-loaded TtDS I bought from a market when I was 10.

This game is a fairly interesting fighter that features a solid roster of Bleach characters from the Soul Society arc. You can either fight online with friends, or play as Komamura and duke it out against three other bots in the game. But the real highlight of the game is its story mode, which does a pretty good job recapping the events of the Agent of the Shinigami arc, then letting you fight your way through the Soul Society arc all the way to Aizen's betrayal.

As someone who picked up this game entirely unaware of the anime, I easily followed along and ended up obsessed with the character designs. Which naturally snowballed into me becoming Bleach's lone and strongest soldier in a sea of One Piece and Naruto fans in school. But with the show wrapping its final episode recently in a beloved way

Let's not beat around the bush, One Piece has too many episodes. So many, that recommending the series can feel like a cruel prank, especially when everyone keeps insisting it gets better as it goes on. Thankfully if you're looking for some cliff notes while dodging the larper accusations, Pirate Warriors 3 does a solid job of squeezing hundreds of episodes into the game.

Kicking things off with Luffy setting out to sea, the game follows the crew all the way through to the Dressrosa arc. I have to admit the game surprised me, as I wasn't expecting a solid story in a game with Dynasty Warriors combat. Maybe that's a testament to One Piece's story as is, but the game does a great job capturing those emotional beats and justifying why fans love Luffy and crew.

Admittedly, a fair bit does get trimmed along the way, but if you're looking to get into the meat of the franchise without getting scared by the volume of content out there, this game is a great place to start.

The Dragon Ball Z series is one of the most important and long-lasting series in the genre of all time. It's been going on for so long, two-hour long YouTube explainer videos still only scrape the surface for the story, which can make approaching it pretty dense. Thankfully, the 2020 Kakarot video game would make the effort and deliver on a pretty refreshing approach to retelling the earliest stories in the series.

Where most anime adaptations have gone the standard 3D arena fighter route, Kakarot instead lets you live through the events through an Action-RPG approach, and covers every major Z saga, from Raditz landing on Earth to the final showdown with Kid Buu.

There's plenty of stuff to do between the fights, which might seem a tad bit like unnecessary padding, but it helps keep the world feel grounded and let's you spend more time with the characters. Plus, what is an RPG without a fishing minigame? You'll also get to fly around the game's many open zones and compete side quests for various characters from the series. It's a pretty refreshing spin for an adaptation, and I'd be open to see other series take a similar approach in the future.

If you've only ever known Dragon Ball through power level memes and Goku screaming for three episodes straight, this is where I'd start. By the time Gohan faces Cell, you'll understand why the series has hung around for four decades.

The Demon Slayer franchise is known for its gorgeous visuals, and somewhat middling storyline, which is why a video game adaptation is a surprising tall order. Surprisingly, this game manages to capture what makes the series so visually captivating, even without Mappa's iconic animation. Demon Slayer: Kimetsu No Yaiba The Hinokami Chronicles depicts an almost shot-for-shot recreation of the anime's entire first season before setting up the eventual Mugen Train arc.

Throughout the game, we follow Tanjiro from Final Selection through Mount Natagumo and onto the train, with light exploration between boss fights built around the series' biggest moments. Much like in the anime, The Rui fight is every bit as striking with a controller in your hands as it was on TV.

Outside of story mode, it's a fairly simple arena fighter, but that works in its favor here. You don't need to be a fighting game expert to see it through, which makes it an easy pick for anyone curious about what all the Demon Slayer fuss was about.

Yes, I know putting a trilogy bundle here seems like a copout, but I can't recommend playing this series any other way. Besides, odds are if you're going to play all the way through the first game, odds are you're likely to want to play through the next two anyway to see where the storyline goes.

The original Ultimate Ninja Storm retells the first Naruto series right up to Naruto and Sasuke's fight at the Valley of the End, with a free-roaming Hidden Leaf Village between battles. Which is a neat point to wrap up on to let Storm 2 focus solely on the Pain arc, which is arguably the most iconic storyline in the series. Storm 3 follows the Fourth Great Ninja War, letting you play out some of the most iconic battles throughout the story.

Like other anime games mentioned before, the boss fights are the centrepiece of these games, and boy do they deliver. Just throw on Linkin Park's 'Numb' and you'll be playing out your very own 480p AMV YouTube clip.

The Ultimate Monarch of Shadows is coming to consoles.

#4045. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4044. Grand Theft Auto VI's Auto Drive Is A Beautiful And Free Version Of Hands-Free Travel

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

This is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

First, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

Next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

Once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I've always enjoyed driving in Grand Theft Auto, but I was grateful to find this almost-hidden option early in the game.

The latest Japanese charts are in from Famitsu, and in perhaps the least surprising debut in recent memory, Grand Theft Auto VI is a hit.

Rockstar's code-in-a-box release had a staggering debut week in Japan, pulling in over 200,000 physical sales and kicking Ocarina of Time's comparatively measly ~35,000 into second. It's shy of the 537,000 Link's latest put up in its debut week, of course, but for a box with no disc in it, it's not bad going.

The rest of the chart is a Switch-fest, mind you, with the likes of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Rhythm Heaven Groove still performing well, and last week's silver medallist, Metaphor: ReFantazio, hanging in there at ninth.

You don't need us to spell it out for you, but that means the PS5 wins the SKU race over the Switch 1 this week. Sony's three systems put up 41,472 total sales, while the Switch, Lite, and OLED combined for 4,362.

#4041. 8 Most Thought-Provoking Messages in GTA 6

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Despite the impression given by its AAA status, humorous style, and mass appeal, Grand Theft Auto has always been an inherently political product, constantly meditating on the real world in each installment.

From American exceptionalism to gang culture, encompassing themes like economic crises, poverty, addiction, and violence, the IP has always been a snapshot of a specific time and place, resonating as a critical work.

Even though many users may want to shy away from its communicative intentions, and even though it's not a revolutionary creation that will change the status quo it denounces, the signs are there, and seeing and interpreting them is part of the experience.

Therefore, in order to honor Rockstar's emphatic attempt to continue this retrospective labor with its latest installment, I invite you to read this list of the eight most thought-provoking messages in GTA 6.

With the phone more prominent than ever in its gameplay mechanics and its own mass surveillance app disguised as a platform to fraternize, it was inevitable that social media would be a focal point of GTA 6's critique.

Snapmatic replicates what we see in apps like Instagram or TikTok: endless content, a permanent notification symbol that prevents you from disconnecting from the site, and the readily available dopamine rush of scrolling before bed or on the bus—all in a rather subtle way.

The game doesn't pressure you to check social media and get hooked on its complex interactive web, because it knows that work has already been done by all these past years of psychological conditioning and addiction tactics that the attention economy has used as factors of production.

The masterful aspect lies in the fact that it plays an identical role with the same characteristics as in real life, enjoying a prodigiously curated algorithm of brain-rot memes, bombastic posts that seek to mask empty lives, and as much postmodernism as Metal Gear Solid 2 could anticipate.

In conjunction with the above, GTA 6's television and radio are the perfect mirror of a society increasingly based on hate, the primary fuel for an algorithm that craves strong emotions, regardless of their nature.

Many of the game's media outlets satirize spaces like the manosphere with a perhaps unintentionally overwhelming precision; they attempt to caricature it, but our reality's malice has become so rampant and exacerbated that it's in this very process of parody that they fully capture it.

If you add to this impressively aggressive and defensive NPCs, trained by the rhetoric of Leonida's propaganda entities that deflect their frustrations onto the scapegoats that are marginalized groups, you get an unfortunate but clear reflection of our times.

Most interactions in the title, whether between the player and its systems or its digital inhabitants, are framed by a disdain inherent to an increasingly intolerant society, which is a curiously relevant tone given the review bombing the game has received for "having a hidden agenda".

Discover the best gym workouts in GTA 6, exercises to avoid, and how water and protein help you get more from your training.

In an era where individualism reigns supreme, the fact that the biggest entertainment product in history offers a love story—even a criminal one—makes an interesting statement about interpersonal relationships today.

Jason and Lucia, like previous protagonists, are outcasts of society who engage in despicable behavior, yet this time cloaked in a notion of love for themselves, their relatives, and even the equally broken friends they make along the way, which is unexpected yet empathetic.

Much of the game's worldbuilding revolves around the systemic violence perpetrated by the vices of our civilization, and in times when cruelty has become the norm, it seems to want to reaffirm that we only have each other to keep going.

I emphasize that it's a naive vision, though it's also a welcome change of tone for a series accustomed to reflecting on violence from an impersonal and apathetic perspective, this time giving more prominence to the human connections that allow us to withstand the onslaught of reality

Leonida, a fitting representation of Florida, is a collage of cultures from every imaginable corner of the globe, transforming each interaction into a world of possibilities that were previously unthinkable due to GTA's deeply American focus.

Therefore, talking to a character, listening to a radio station, or accepting a side mission has acquired a more diverse background, as the protagonists of these sequences represent every continent on Earth.

GTA 6 doesn't just speak to the United States, but to its version as the epicenter of countless nationalities and ethnicities, which is a more accurate representation of its reality, thus being more fun and exciting.

And that, I believe, is a powerful message in itself, because the experience improves substantially when you shop in European stores, eat Latin American or Asian food, and listen to African music, just as it is in real life.

Find a fighter jet in GTA 6, learn how to enter Mile Zero Air Station, and escape the five-star wanted level after stealing one.

Our relationship with violence in video games has been a subject of debate for years, with numerous attempts, such as Hotline Miami, Spec Ops: The Line, and The Last of Us Part II, to show us that it's more than just depleting the invisible health points of a bunch of pixels.

However, given GTA 6's technical and realistic level, the conversation turns even more uncomfortable, as the feeling of attacking sentient beings is so palpable that unleashing violence for no reason feels extremely unsettling.

Robbing everyone, shooting all heads in sight, or punching even the air itself ceases to be fun and becomes an action with consequences as real as a video game can currently offer, which explains why many don't feel as comfortable doing the same things they did in GTA 5.

Was seeing such a faithfully crafted simulation of our reality what we needed to understand the messages conveyed by the aforementioned games? Perhaps, but the fact that interactive violence only disgusts us when we see ourselves reflected in it demonstrates the inherent lack of empathy we have had in the past within the medium.

After the 2008 financial crisis, a global pandemic, and numerous armed conflicts that flirt with the possibility of a third world war, citizens around the world face a future that looks bleak from every angle.

You study, you work every day, you exercise, you fight to maintain your relationships, but always knowing that the most likely outcome of such a titanic effort is mere survival, and perhaps not even that is guaranteed.

Like Jason and Lucia, you are overwhelmed by the undeniable impossibility of climbing the economic ladder. However, unlike Jason and Lucia, you don't resort to robberies, mass heists, and drug dealing; instead, you turn to GTA 6.

The game becomes a fantasy not by offering opulence, but by presenting a life where you can have a home and a family, aspirations increasingly unattainable for current generations, who experience the game's mundane aspects firsthand, not the exciting ones.

We can also scroll endlessly, deadlift, and eat lots of empanadas, yet the dreams of yesterday that fueled the efforts of so many are now a distant legend because dreaming itself has become a privilege.

Find a tank at Mile Zero Air Station in GTA 6. Learn where to enter the base, where the tanks are parked, and what to expect when you escape.

GTA 6 is full of homeless people, drug addicts, criminals, corrupt cops, manipulative public figures, burnt-out workers, and countless other demographics that, thanks to technological capabilities, finally allow Rockstar to say what they've been hinting at for years: true violence comes from the system.

Media monopolies that print fake news to promote divisive narratives, security forces that enforce the law only when it benefits the powerful, algorithmic industries that suck up attention and quell dissent, politicians who answer to lobbyists rather than the people...

With all this in mind, GTA 6 proposes an interesting dichotomy: is violence perpetrated by the person who robs at gunpoint or protests by burning a dumpster, or by the system that subjugates them so that their highest aspiration is to work themselves to death?

Taking your destiny into your own hands, the game echoes, is only viable illegally, since the law is no longer designed to benefit the commons. It doesn't morally absolve them, nor us as players, though at least it bothers to question who is ultimately responsible for the oppressive existence we're stuck in.

Throughout the game, you experience a simulation of another life that, nevertheless, closely resembles your own. You have to do chores, take care of yourself, actively and thoughtfully connect with your loved ones, and work towards finding your place in this world, and those aren't always easy tasks.

I don't believe that GTA 6, contrary to what sensationalist journalists might claim, intends to lead young people into a life of crime, but rather to encourage them to recognize society's current state of affairs and navigate its waters as it unfolds.

You can't prevent war crimes, a sustained rise in the price index, the decline of cognitive abilities due to AI, or the complete disintegration of the collective fabric induced by social media, yet you can understand that all of this exists and stand against it.

Living is the most special probabilistic event of all, and surrendering this privilege to feed a slavish routine is admitting defeat. If in GTA 6 you can stay healthy, organize yourself, help your loved ones, and engage in activities that nourish you, you can do so in real life as well.

And no, a AAA game isn't going to spark an insurrection, but if it can at least encourage reflection in new generations, let it be in a fruitful direction, aligned with what it aims to communicate, not with what the fatalists claim.

Grand Theft Auto 6 puts a large emphasis on keeping your relationship sound, so you need to know what ways are the best to raise the romance between Jason and Lucia.

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4038. 8 PS2 JRPGs That Reward Players for Exploring the World More Than Grinding Levels

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

Back in the day, JRPGs relied too much on grinding before letting us progress further into the adventure, either by earning experience or amassing gold. SNES games were the biggest offenders, even though some already featured optional dungeons, secrets, and promoted exploring way more than grinding. PS1 JRPGs doubled down on this, with many games letting us explore a sprawling overworld in search of benefits.

Now, in the PS2? Well, we have way more titles that reward players for taking their time exploring the world, its systems, and its features, rather than mindlessly grinding by beating the same enemies over and over again. I've picked some games I personally played and believe that the exploration pays off beautifully in the long run compared to battling over and over again.

Dark Cloud introduced a town-building mechanic called Georama, which the protagonist must interact with to move the story forward. In Dark Cloud 2, the feature was expanded, and you need to engage much more intimately with the system if you want to advance in the game. That alone already requires you to explore dungeons in search of more Geostones.

A list of ten Xbox 360 JRPGs that focused on rewarding players for exploration over grinding out levels.

If you want to achieve 100% completion in each town, you will be awarded special rewards. To do so, Max will need to take photos to transform his ideas into new inventions. It is a pretty neat feature, and although it will not strengthen you directly, it will certainly make your playthrough more enjoyable and immersive.

In a game that lacks a traditional level system, it is pretty obvious that grinding for levels would be non-rewarding. Romancing SaGa: Minstrel Song still has a modicum of grinding, and you can strengthen your characters in battle by increasing their attributes bit by bit. However, doing this while neglecting quests and events is a recipe for failure, because enemies' Battle Rank will rise steadily, and if you are not prepared, your life will get complicated.

I know a friend who practically suffered a softlock in Romancing SaGa: Minstrel Song. He didn't know the series' intricacies and ground-level mechanics, so he played like a traditional RPG instead of exploring the Free Scenario structure, recruiting new characters, or evolving Classes and Skills. At one point, common encounters were harder than bosses, and because he hadn't kept pace with enemy progression, he fell completely behind.

Anyone who has ever played Suikoden knows that the biggest chunk of the game's fun and progression is tied to its characters. Every entry features 108 members to recruit into the resistance, and most provide a tangible benefit, whether unlocking a new facility, adding a gameplay feature, or joining as new combatants in battle.

Regardless, you will want a full roster because it elevates and improves the entire Suikoden experience. You get new storylines, a better ending, and overall enhanced enjoyment when you recruit the full cast. Since leveling in Suikoden is gated by the region you are in, traditional grinding becomes virtually impossible, making exploration the far better path. I chose Suikoden V because the fourth game isn't one of the fan favorites, though you can certainly play that one too.

For anyone who loves or thinks the number of recruitable characters in Suikoden is massive, meet Radiata Stories, which offers over 170 members. Granted, you cannot get everyone in a single playthrough because Radiata Stories splits into two narratives at a certain point, but how much you accomplish in one run depends entirely on your willingness to explore. Most characters are found through optional endeavors and side activities, so you may need a walkthrough.

Once you recruit someone, they join at different levels, each with their own weapon and skills. Sometimes you may need to grind if a low-level character joins your ranks, but doing so will also bolster the link system, which lets all party members share skills. That is why exploring and adding more characters to your roster is so vital, letting you enjoy the benefits of linking to the utmost.

Wild Arms 2 added an overworld mechanic that you either love or hate: the search system. Towns and dungeons don't appear on the world map automatically, so you have to actively scan for them to show up. Wild Arms 3 expanded upon this idea. For those who enjoy the search system, it is a pretty great mechanic that can surprise curious players with hidden treasures and extra locations.

From Chained Echoes to Octopath Traveler II, these JRPGs on the Switch are more about exploring the overworld than mindlessly grinding levels.

Also, completionists hunting down all the EX File Keys will need to follow specific coordinates closely (or, well, just look up a walkthrough). There are also Millennium Puzzles, Migrant Seals, and plenty of treasure chests scattered around. Plus, with the Encounter Gauge system, you can avoid random battles for the most part, and if you are strong enough, skip them altogether while exploring the desert world of Filgaia.

One of my biggest regrets in my JRPG journey was going for the platinum trophy in Rogue Galaxy. By the time I realized it was a total drag, I was already too invested, falling into the classic sunk cost fallacy. One trophy required reaching level 99 with any character, which was utterly unnecessary since I defeated practically every boss around level 70, including the Ghost Ship.

All that is to say that levels matter in Rogue Galaxy, but they aren't the deciding factor. The game's progression system hinges on the Revelation Flow, which you unlock by placing specific items found in treasure chests, enemy drops, and exploration. I know weapon synthesis does demand a bit of combat before you can fuse two weapons, though you never truly need to grind. You can simply play naturally and synthesize as you go, and it gets even better if you keep exploring to find stronger base weapons to use as materials.

Final Fantasy XII was the first entry in the series to give the sensation of an open world to explore right from the get-go, provided you could survive the bites of a stray dinosaur. The game features standard levels, which are nice, but most of your real strength comes from the License Board and buying gear. However, you only earn gil by selling loot, and selling specific loot combinations also unlocks neat equipment in the Bazaar.

That is why mindlessly fighting the same type of enemy isn't particularly advantageous in Final Fantasy XII, whereas a focused hunt for specific drops or maintaining a high battle chain pays off hugely. Additionally, Ivalice is packed with optional areas, hidden Espers, and some truly wacky secret treasures that practically require a guide to track down. Trust me, you will make your resistance members far stronger by knowing what you are doing and exploring thoroughly rather than simply bulldozing ahead.

I feel like Breath of Fire: Dragon Quarter is such an unorthodox title that it could easily make most lists of JRPGs that refuse to fit into a standard mold. The thing is, it plays far more like a roguelike than a traditional RPG, and if you know anything about roguelikes, you know traditional grinding is completely useless. In fact, you cannot even grind in Dragon Quarter, especially once you unlock the D-Counter and watch your remaining percentage tick away like sand through your fingers.

What you must do instead is constantly search for items, open chests, save up money, and bank party XP, because when you die - and you probably will - you can restart the game carrying stronger gear, stored XP, and access to the SOL replay feature to uncover more of the world's story. It is an extra bonus if your D-Rank rises, as you will gain access to brand-new rooms and collect even more loot, making your trek to the surface much more favorable.

Discover eight SNES JRPGs that reward exploration over grinding, from Chrono Trigger and Terranigma to Final Fantasy VI and Lufia II.

#4036. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4035. Poll: Are You Still Happy To Pay For Online Multiplayer On Xbox Consoles?

I'm not sure paid multiplayer makes sense anymore

Paying for access to online multiplayer has been the norm on Xbox consoles for decades now. It's something we've come to expect as part of playing online with friends and other folk around the world. The general understanding is, if you don't have Xbox Live, you're not playing online.

Eight years ago, I bought a gaming laptop to play Battlefield V on the go, and ever since paying for access to online multiplayer hasn't made much sense to me. It's just not something you do on PC. Sure, games like World of Warcraft and Final Fantasy XIV require additional subscriptions in order to play, but the majority of online games, like BFV, only require you to upfront the retail cost and crack on.

Xbox Play Anywhere is probably where console paywalls really start to look silly. Just a few months ago, I bought Subnautica 2 to play with a friend through the Xbox PC app. I could've opted for Steam, but I wanted to work towards those Xbox cheevos (when they eventually arrive). For a couple of weeks, I'd hop on the PC and dive into alien waters with my mate.

One day, I fancied playing on the big screen in my living room, so I installed Subnautica 2 on my Xbox Series X, booted it up and was prompted to buy a Game Pass subscription just to play the same save file I'd been enjoying for weeks through the Xbox PC app. Like I said, a bit silly.

Time went on, and I'd more or less let this go from my head until I read a report from Windows Central a couple days ago, claiming that Microsoft's upcoming Xbox Helix next-gen console could have plans to kill paywalls for paid multiplayer.

"Sources close to Microsoft's plans tell me Xbox Helix was originally conceived as a true console-PC hybrid with access to Windows PC games and stores such as Steam, alongside another major change: no paywall for online multiplayer."

According to Jez Corden, the original plan for Xbox Helix was to create a console-PC hybrid with access to Steam, potentially spelling the end of Xbox's staple multiplayer charges. It kind of makes sense when you think about it. If you can play your Xbox games across both console and PC, whether through disc-to-digital or Xbox Play Anywhere, it seems like pointless friction to lock multiplayer behind a paywall depending on which device you're playing on.

Back in 2021, changes to Xbox's paid multiplayer requirements allowed players without an active Xbox Live Gold subscription to access multiplayer free-to-play titles such as Fortnite, Call of Duty: Warzone and Apex Legends. And today, Xbox Live Gold isn't even a thing, as it's been absorbed into Xbox Game Pass.

So, even if Xbox Helix's original vision has changed somewhat from what Corden initially reported, it's still not out of the question to suggest that paid multiplayer could eventually become redundant.

#4033. The Video Games You Should Play This Weekend – November 20, 2026

This is it. We finally made it. Grand Theft Auto VI is here. I have played the game for a number of hours and read Matt Miller's glowing review, which you can read here, and I still don't know if I personally believe the game is actually out. But that just might the lack of sleep from staying up late to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

Many games chose to avoid the blast radius of Rockstar's latest crime caper, but that doesn't mean it's the only game that came out this week and you can find them below. But as is tradition, here are some of our top stories of the week first.

If you’re not aware that GTAVI launched this week, it’s possible that you’ve been living under a rock somewhere. Nonetheless, we’re here to offer the reminder that after more than a decade of waiting for a new installment, Rockstar has this week rolled out its new game. It’s good. Like, really good, and if you’re an adult who plays video games, it should really be a title you make time for.

In my review, I highlighted some of its many positive traits, but as you prepare to dive into its criminal delights over the weekend, one element I’d especially like to point out is its viability as a game to play with your partner. Like an excellent prestige TV crime show, GTAVI is a game that features a rich, dramatic, funny, and well-written story that I genuinely believe has the potential to be a good time for both a player and a viewer, though, admittedly, the person who gets to enjoy running the sticks is probably having the most fun.

However you plan to enjoy it, here’s hoping Grand Theft Auto VI turns out to be worth the wait you’ve likely had for it. For my part, it certainly has been, and I suspect you’ll find it only gets better the deeper into the game you go.

The running joke publisher Devolver Digital has made with this “spectacular remaster of the original remake of the unreleased action-platformer starring the most famous video game mascot of all time” is that it launched the same day as Grand Theft Auto VI. Volvy’s Adventure has been positioned as a tongue-in-cheek competitor to Rockstar’s behemoth, with Devovler even releasing a trailer that is a shot-for-shot parody of GTA VI’s. While I’ve chuckled at these stunts, Volvy’s Adventure isn’t just a joke game. It’s actually pretty fun.

For one, it’s developed by a respectable studio in Doinksoft, the team behind fun indie games like Gato Roboto, Gunbrella, and this year’s Dark Scrolls. Vovly’s Adventure is a 16-bit 2D platformer where players use Volvy’s oversized fist to punch through objects, which, in turn, propels him in the same direction. Thus, platforming is a fast-paced and explosive exercise in soaring fist-first through barriers and enemies, collecting items, and burrowing through certain platforms. The platforming feels pretty good, and it’s backed by a catchy soundtrack; the destruction is satisfying; and the levels are relatively brief, making it easy to plow through.

I wasn’t sure what to expect from Volvy’s Adventure beyond the marketing jokes, but it’s got some sauce. Sitting at the budget price of $5 (and a launch discount of $3.74), it’s a curiosity that’s easy to check out.

Australia Did It, from Rami Ismail and his team at Aesthetician Labs, hit a little snag with its publicized release date. Valve got backed up approving the release of games on its platform and a handful of games were affected. Australia Did It, despite the unexpected delay, is out... and it's good! Here's what Brian Shea wrote in his review: "Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world."

God of War Sons of Sparta is... underwhelming, to be blunt. You can read my review here. The game is a prequel where you play as a young Kratos and go on a 2D Metroid-inspired adventure with your brother, Deimos. If you are interested in getting the full God of War story, there are some interesting narrative and character details in the game, but it has some shortcomings. What's surprising about its re-release this week is that it is now available on PS4. An unexpected "new" platform to say the least.
