#3921. Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

It's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

It's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

In a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

New Radical Games has had its unannounced project canceled according to a developer, with the studio speculated to have been working on a The Simpsons: Hit & Run remake.

Earlier this year, Simpsons creator Matt Groening casually dropped the news that something to do with The Simpsons: Hit & Run was happening, saying at a D23 panel that "the original game is coming back in some form." This, mixed with New Radical's now-deleted LinkedIn hiring post that mentioned "our stylized game" which would naturally fit with The Simpsons, had folks speculating that the studio – partially comprised of devs from OG Hit & Run studio, Radical Entertainment – might be working on a remake.

However, whatever the studio was working on has now unfortunately been scrapped. Darren Evenson – senior game designer at New Radical Games – posts on LinkedIn saying the devs' latest project "was part of a whole gaggle of cancellations."

While The Simpsons link is still unconfirmed, Evenson writes "if you don't make the money, then you don't get the power" which is a reference to Scarface – which Radical also worked on a game for. However, this line was famously parodied in The Simpsons when Homer has his giant pile of sugar in the backyard. I could be reading entirely too much into it, but that could be a hint that this was sadly a Hit & Run remaster that was canned.

Needless to say, fans aren't happy. "I'm never going to emotionally recover from this," one says on Twitter in response. "Yeah bro is paraphrasing a quote from Homer it's over boys," speculates another.

There's no wonder the news is having such an impact, even without confirmation that a remake was definitely canceled. Sure, GTA 6 is the highest-rated game of all time and people were waiting 13 years for it to come out, but after 23 years, The Simpsons Hit & Run was the real open-world car-stealing game that everyone was waiting to see get a follow-up.

The iconic licensed title is still one of the most beloved games ever made, and fans have been asking for a sequel for decades, but despite its massive success – and reports emerging that there was a sequel in the works – one never came to fruition. The unrelated The Simpsons Game was the only console game the franchise has had since.

#3919. Only two days out from GTA 6, its publisher Take-Two lay off staff at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis

About a third of the workforce has been cut, reportedly

Upsettingly, it is that time of the week again, as Take-Two are laying off staff at Firaxis, the developer behind Civilization and XCOM, only a little over a year the last time the studio suffered from layoffs. Firaxis are, notably, owned by Take-Two, the publisher of GTA 6 which comes out in, oh, two days time? Interesting timing, 'ey.

Word of the layoffs came from Bloomberg, who report that about 60 people are losing their jobs, apparently roughly a third of its staff. The studio's head, Heather Hazen, is also leaving. A spokesperson for 2K Games (the Take-Two label that manages Firaxis) shared a statement on the layoffs: "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years.

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis." I don't feel personally confident in the idea that the only way to make a company succeed is by laying a bunch of people off thereby making it much harder to make anything in the first place, especially in the lead-up to what will likely be the best selling game of the decade, but what do I know!

Bloomberg also report Firaxis have been working on a new XCOM, which is yet to be announced, but the project has apparently had to contend with numerous development issues, missing a "significant milestone over the summer." This new XCOM game hasn't been cancelled at the very least, but anonymous sources that spoke with Bloomberg said it may have to deal with a shakeup due to the cuts. As always, solidarity with all those affected by this situation.

#3916. The Witcher 4 Is Not a PS5 Exclusive, CDPR Clarifies After Sony Deal

Did anyone really think The Witcher 4 was going to be a PS5 exclusive?

For those who missed it, CDPR confirmed yesterday that it has signed a marketing deal with Sony on its upcoming RPG.

While the details are light, it’s expected this will take the same shape as PlayStation’s arrangement with GTA 6, where the title’s promoted “like” an exclusive – even though it’s technically not.

But it seems there was some confusion online about the nature of Sony’s deal, which CEO Michal Nowakowski has now clarified on social media.

“We’re looking forward to our partnership with PlayStation! And just to be clear: The Witcher 4 and our other upcoming titles will remain multiplatform.”

It’s as expected really, but Nowakowski still faced follow-up questions about whether Ciri’s story may launch first on PS5, before other platforms.

“All the platforms release at the same time: PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. No one gets left behind.”

Of course, this is all entirely as expected – the original comments mentioned a marketing deal only, and I don’t think Sony could afford to keep a game as big as The Witcher 4 off other platforms, to be brutally honest.

It does hopefully mean the game will be optimised for the PS5, though, taking advantage of unique features like the DualSense et al.

I’m sure we’ll learn a lot more about how Sony and CDPR are collaborating once we get closer to the game’s release.

Historically, the PC store, GOG (Good Old Games) was created by CD Projekt, the Polish company best known for The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077. GOG launched in 2008 as a digital storefront focused on classic PC games and a "DRM-free philosophy", and it operated as part of the CD Projekt Group for over 17 years.

A lot of CD Projekt's games were sold on GOG, and GOG became well known for selling games 'without' DRM (Digital Rights Management) and for keeping older games working on modern PCs.

GOG has expressed interest in bringing back physical PC games, particularly the classic "big box" style releases.

So you'll find that while PlayStation as of 2027 (or whenever it is) no longer allows you have a physical game or DRM free; PC & Nintendo has much better ownership & DRM policies.

The situation is different now, CD Project RED learned from the Cyberpunk 2077 launch. They were using their own proprietary REDengine 4, which is a PC-first engine where console ports require a large amount of effort to get running and well optimized.

Now they are using Unreal Engine 5, which is a 3rd party engine built specifically for multi-platform releases. By design the engine takes care of many console porting efforts as it's an integral part of the engine. A developer from CD Project RED mentioned during a recent event that they are now designing games around the specifications of consoles rather than high-end PCs (like they did for Cyberpunk 2077).

So expect The Witcher 4 to run like any other Unreal Engine 5 game released recently (Clair Obscur Expedition 33, Saros, Silent Hill 2, Phantom Blade Zero, The Blood of Dawnwalker) on current platforms.

@TrollOfWar As a developer, I'm not only very familiar with Unreal Engine, I'm tremendously aware of how terrible it has been of late to work with effectively and efficiently.

I don't know of a developer or development team who is happy with the state of Unreal Engine right now. At this point I would assume those that are, are legally obliged to say so, or are receiving some financial benefit as a team for being aligned with it.

There is no such thing as a PC first engine, all game development engines run on PC first, and are built and incorporated around the implementation of console runtime environments using either SDK tools, Xbox/Nintendo/Sony DevTools or a combination of all or next to none.

As some terribly low budget Dev's will not have the SDK, select a drop down in Unity/Unreal Engine, export to the console and then have assistance from a platform suggested studio that assists, or an internal onboarding team.

So, a PC first engine simply means the developers are focused heavily on PC development as their primary bread and butter, it has nothing to do with the engine capabilities.

Unreal Engine itself is one of the most famous examples of PC first, as its engine literally was and is built around PC first ideology within development.

It's just marketed differently depending on which page of their site you click, which rep you speak to and so forth.

By going from REDengine, over to Unreal Engine, CDPR have not done so due to the ease at which they can deliver on console environments, it's due to the fact they clearly don't have the in-house technical staff to assist with incorporating all that is needed in a real-time environment into their engine. At least in an ongoing fashion during development, especially due to the dawn of at least 2-4 new consoles arriving in a year or two.

The issue is that Unreal Engine can be modified somewhat, it can be altered ad-hoc, yet ultimately all substantial feature sets and abilities are governed by their internal team of "specialists".

Lumen, Nanite, both wonderful, developers didn't get to implement that ahead of time, they didn't get to pick the time frame, they didn't get to choose how it speaks to the rest of the engine.

You lose a lot, a hell of a lot going from a very established, very capable engine runtime environment that your entire studio have spent years tailoring, to then go to an off the shelf solution with little to no say on the next major features and how they work alongside other tools.

There's a reason Pixar use Marionette and Render Man, it's not because it's easier, it's because every step of the way they get to not have to ask another company if they can "Please Sir have some more".

CDPR going from in house to off the shelf does not show they have learned anything, it shows their team quite literally don't know how to develop and maintain an in house engine during development of a cross-generational release.

People can believe what they think of the marketing speak, but I implore people to remember that we coming off the back of a few years of very terribly console optimised versions of releases that have indeed used Unreal Engine ... a PC first engine as they all are.

I will believe CDPR made the right decision for them when they prove it, up until now they have done everything but to the industry and consumers.

@ButteredCrumpet Interesting post. But I think there's a few things worth highlighting.

The main reason CDPR switched to Unreal Engine was stated in their debrief about why CyberPunk 2077 was delayed three times, and why even then it STILL came out in a poor state that required years of development to get it up to scratch. Their primary conclusions were related to the RED Engine, staff turnover and the issues these caused. (CDPR are very open and this was all in their investor calls)

That's not to say the RED Engine was bad, it isn't, but new staff would not be familiar with it, nor their custom tools, and many of their best devs would have to spend time getting the new staff up to speed, rather than actually working on the game. This slowed the whole process down considerably and reportedly caused some top staff to leave, which also didn't help. But it was made even worse because they also had a high staff turnover - for a variety of reasons - and so this process would repeat again and again, slowing progress to a crawl.

Interestingly 343 Industries came to exactly the same conclusion in their debrief as to why Halo Infinite was delayed a year, why it launched in an incomplete state, and again took years to bring many features expected at launch. Same conclusion: Bespoke engine and the issues this caused with a high staff turnover, hence they also decided to go UE5 before Halo was moved to Activision.

TLDR: Ultimately the decision for both studios was that for all the potential downsides of Unreal Engine the pros outweighed the cons.

What's particularly interesting is it isn't really about the technical capability of the engines, while that would have been a consideration, it's more about the people making it and the actual management issues of that when scaling up for these massive projects.

As the old saying goes, the best tool is the one you actually use.

The issue is that Unreal Engine can be modified somewhat

UE5 is almost entirely modular. You don't like the physics model, you don't like the lighting, the rendering or even major features like Lumen or Nanite you can replace them all.

Obviously at some point it makes no sense to, you might be better off building your own engine.

It will be interesting to see how CDPR will adapt UE5 for their uses. Like you I was slightly sceptical about using UE5 but will wait to see before judging. But I think it's fair to say most studios that release on UE5 don't have their own Engine Programmers who built something as complex as RED Engine, CDPR do, so they should be able to make the engine run better than most.

UPDATE: They even mentioned when working with Epic on the Witcher 4 demo that they had fixed some traversal stuttering bugs and sent those fixes back to Epic. CDPR aren't just licensing UE5, the engineers are rewriting core engine pipelines and contributing those fixes back into public versions of UE5 for the benefit of all developers.

#3915. What would Rockstar have done if GTA hadn't taken off? Former tech director Obbe Vermeij on Scottish zombies, James Bond and the "curse" of success

"We ended up just cutting and cutting it."

It's bizarre today to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't Grand Theft Auto. Frankly, it's bizarre to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't GTA 6, which rolls onto console hard drives this week. A decade in the making, with a development team of thousands scattered across an international network of studios, GTA 6 aims to be the Maximum Game. It's both a dense, lively open world and a monument to the exhausting impersonality of "triple-A" game productions. It contains multitudes: birdlife! Realistic cloud formation! Fuel mechanics! Romance! Soda visibly sloshing around in bottles! It's an imperial production shadowed by labour disputes, that appears to have given Rockstar's various teams little time or space to think about anything else.

It wasn't ever thus. Once upon a time, Rockstar weren't just known for GTA and to a considerably lesser extent, Red Dead Redemption. Once upon a time, they had a reputation for slightly dodgy experiments. I recently interviewed former Rockstar North tech director Obbe Vermeij about a few of them, including Agent, the unofficial James Bond game Rockstar toyed with before putting all chips on Grand Theft Auto 5.

During the noughties especially, when the most expensive games took considerably less time to make, Rockstar tried their hand at a number of projects besides GTA. There was 2002's Manhunt, a rancid parody of snuff films – not much loved, but sufficiently admired to spawn a sequel in the hands of Rockstar London. There was 2005's adaptation of Walter Hill flick The Warriors - a mouthy Homeric beat 'em up in which you cross New York on foot over the course of a single night - and 2006's Rockstar Presents Table Tennis - an inexplicable pivot towards realistic sports simulation from Rockstar San Diego. Later in 2006 came Bully, aka Canis Canem Edit, a boarding school life sim from Rockstar Vancouver (née Barking Dog Studios). I didn't warm to Bully, myself, but I've never been able to get its sardonic OST out of my head.

In amongst all these, Rockstar weighed up several game projects that never made it out of the building. The aforesaid Agent is perhaps the best-known, but my conversation with Vermeij (who worked at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009) began with "Z", a fleeting attempt to expand into the world of zombie action games, which Rockstar spent a few weeks mulling over in the wake of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. It was set in the islands of Scotland, which would have made it the only Rockstar North project to unfold in the studio's backyard. "I think it was meant to be smaller than GTA, map-wise, and there weren't going to be any deserted cities - it was really just islands and some villages," Vermeij told me. "But it really didn't get that far."

The pitch for Z couldn't be further from the sweat and glitter of GTA 6's Miami, but the two projects would have shared a taste for 'simulation' elements. "It actually was going to have cars running out of fuel," Vermeij told me. "That was going to be one of the things, and the whole idea was that you'd find cars and they'd only have a little bit of fuel in them." As for why Z never entered full development, turns out desolate North Atlantic archipelagos full of corpses can be a bit of a downer. "Everybody was super excited to do something new," Vermeij went on. "And then pretty quickly, we kind of realised that it's really just a depressing version of GTA, and it sort of died."

The increasing success of Grand Theft Auto during these years was something of a "curse", Vermeij went on. It meant that a lot of Rockstar's ventures beyond GTA were eventually folded back into the series. "It's very difficult to have a studio and have one mega game, and then do something on the side," he explained. "It's almost impossible, because at any time during the development of the smaller project, management's going to say 'oh! The big project's in trouble. We need more people.' And they're just going to pull everybody from that small team onto the big team, so even if we had progressed with [Z], what would have happened is we would have had to start GTA 4 at the same time, and eventually the small team would just be merged with the big team again."

Rockstar's Bondalike game Agent got a lot further down the road to release than Z. It was in development for several years following GTA 4's launch, and was touted by co-founder Sam Houser as Rockstar's next megagame. "A lot of work had been done on that," Vermeij recalled. "And then we ended up just cutting and cutting it, because the same thing happened – at some point you kind of go OK, well, we better get on with the next GTA."

Agent sounds like it could have been a hoot, at least going by Vermeij's description of his own time with the project. It was a relatively linear, level-based action game with a touch of camp. "There was a French ski resort, and there was going to be a Mediterranean town like San Tropez, somewhere like that," Vermeij explained. "There was going to be a North African place, like Morocco or Egypt. The last level was going to be on the moon, with lasers – like Moonraker. There was another one, London or something, I can't remember. But then we just ended up cutting everything down, because what we could see happening was that at some point, we would have to go back to work on GTA. It wasn't close to being finished."

While never a spoof in the vein of Austin Powers, Agent would have been a sillier production than the grimy and downbeat GTA 4. "It was meant to lean into all the cliches," Vermeij said. "It was like James Bond from the 1970s - there was a girl with white boots. It wasn't a comedy, it was just completely over-the-top cliched."

As for the choice of a level-based format, this came from a desire for variety the studio couldn't realistically achieve in a GTA-style open world. "If you had to have them all on one map, you would basically have had to model a mini version of Europe," Vermeij said, "So you couldn't do that." Players might have been able to revisit locations containing several missions, which calls to mind Io Interactive's later Hitman: World of Assassination games, to say nothing of their own bash at the Flemingverse, 007 First Light. "I don't how whether it was going to be completely linear, or whether you were always going to be able to visit all those locations." Vermeij said.

Needless to say, Rockstar's Bondalike would have featured chase scenes. Vermeij himself worked on the moving parts. "I remember doing some work on what we called the car recording stuff for GTA," he went on. "So if a level designer wanted to set up a chase scene, they would drive one car, record it, and then play back the recording, drive a second car and record that... and so driving one by one, you could set up a whole chase scene. I did a version of that for [human] characters as well, because for one of the Agent missions in the French ski resort, there was like a chase where the bad guys were on skiis and using their machine guns. So I set up a thing where you'd play them one by one, and then play the whole thing back. There was maybe like five or six bad guys and they'd ski after you, and then it was just up to the player to avoid them."

According to Vermeij, Agent never had a defined story during his time with it. It was more of a mix of scenario concepts, "kind of how we used to do games with GTA 3 and Vice City". Mind you, the absence of a nailed-down plot isn't necessarily a sign that Agent was lightyears from being finished. Even at their most byzantine, Bond movie plotlines often feel like an afterthought. "It's like oh yeah, there's a bad guy and there's a thingally-dingally that needs to be captured before the world comes to an end," summarised Vermeij. Still, Agent would spend a long time in limbo after Vermeij left. It's still unclear how much it was in active development before Rockstar's trademark finally evaporated in November 2018.

One thing I learned while reading up on Rockstar's checkered history was that GTA 3, the game that made GTA a Thing on PlayStation, wasn't deemed an immediate hit at launch. According to Vermeij himself, it was months before Rockstar realised what they'd built. This inspired an obvious closing question: what might Rockstar have done, if GTA 3 hadn't blown up the way it did? Which of those other projects might have become the focus?

"I really have never thought about it," Vermeij pondered. "When Rockstar San Diego joined, it was 2002, and they already had a bunch of games and a bunch of franchises, like Midnight Club and Smuggler's Run. They were already into driving games and city games in that way, so it wouldn't have surprised me if we'd gone in that direction anyway. But then they were more about car modding and decals and stuff like that.

"At Rockstar North, we only had Manhunt and GTA," he went on. "With Manhunt, that team was in development hell for a while, they had a couple of rough years where they got stuck and in the end, they pulled through, and they got a pretty decent game. But I don't think that would have been the future. I don't think [Rockstar North] would have done a Manhunt 2. So yeah, it would be Table Tennis, I think! Everything on Table Tennis!"

#3914. Doctor Strange 2 explores the multiverse, but its Doomsday legacy is proving Marvel can fix mistakes

On the road to Avengers: Doomsday, Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness offered a masterclass in course correction

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On the road to Avengers: Doomsday, the multiverse is a touch too familiar. But back in 2022, our expectations were limitless as the walls broke down between several cinematic universes amid Disney's acquisition of Fox.

So, who better than the Sorcerer Supreme to tap into the magic of that concept alongside a handful of genius what-if castings and a deliciously evil villain in Scarlet Witch?

But even before cameras began rolling, there was an obvious issue. A movie called Multiverse of Madness has to live up to the promise of its title. The Doctor Strange sequel certainly delivered on that potential from the outset by installing Evil Dead and Spider-Man's Sam Raimi as director. Already, Marvel had a winning hand – and Raimi made it count. After Loki and Spider-Man: No Way Home cracked open the door to alternate worlds inside the MCU, Doctor Strange 2 swept across planets and fired through different realities – ensuring a comic book movie played out, well, actually like a comic book for once. Groundbreaking, I know.

This being Sam Raimi, though, there's a playful mix of horror and heartache alongside the trippy visuals. Scarlet Witch may be the focus, but Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness was propelled along by Stephen Strange's reluctance to let Rachel McAdams' Christine Palmer, the love of his life, go for good. This isn't Peter Parker and MJ's will they/won't they romance, but a more mature way for a hero to realize he doesn't always get the girl and hits harder than I expected upon a rewatch.

On top of the emotion, there was a generous helping of fan service, largely thanks to Earth-838's Illuminati.

Patrick Stewart once again taking a seat as Professor Xavier feels especially welcome in the weeks since the actor's passing, while the rest of the group tasked with staving off multiversal threats – Captain Carter, Black Bolt, Lashana Lynch's Captain Marvel, Baron Mordo, and John Krasinski's Mister Fantastic – were a grab bag of fancasting favorites and second chances that harnessed the creative brilliance of the multiverse.

Welcome to Road to Doomsday, GamesRadar+'s weekly MCU rewatch series. Over 15 weeks, we'll be revisiting each Marvel movie and TV show on Disney's list of essential movies to watch ahead of Avengers: Doomsday, sharing our thoughts upon rewatching and deciphering what we can learn about the next Marvel mega-event from each entry. Why not relive some MCU highlights and watch along with us?

Elsewhere, Scarlet Witch is a strange case – no pun intended – in Multiverse of Madness. Elizabeth Olsen openly admitted to being the only real authority to the movie's creatives about how her character arc went in WandaVision (she finished filming the Disney Plus series just days prior to production beginning on the Doctor Strange sequel). While the hunt for her children across realities made sense in theory, it becomes too huge of a leap for someone who was at least coming to terms with her losses by the end of her time in Westview.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

It all culminated in a death that was dramatically heavy, but left her family – and the audience – with too many loose ends and a gnawing sense of loss across Agatha All Along and VisionQuest.

But dead doesn't always mean dead in comic book movies. In the grand scheme of the MCU, Scarlet Witch's demise was keenly felt, even if we collectively knew it wasn't necessarily permanent.

The decision to retcon her inevitable revival into a way to entrench Doctor Doom's position as the next Big Bad of the multiverse was an inspired one.

Enter Doctor Doom. In the VisionQuest post-credits scene, Robert Downey Jr.'s masked supervillain arrives at the ruins of the Darkhold Castle in Mount Wundagore to resurrect Wanda and claim her powers for his own twisted quest to save the multiverse. In one fell swoop, it makes the end of Multiverse of Madness and what comes next in Avengers: Doomsday all the more interesting – not least because we know just how powerful Scarlet Witch is in the MCU. Doom already has Hulk and Scarlet Witch on his side, with Spider-Man possibly on his radar too. Turning some of Marvel's most iconic heroes against the Avengers (via fair means or foul) would open up far more narrative possibilities than an all-against-Doom battle.

Avengers: Doomsday sounds like the darkest Marvel movie yet, which is why it needs a pinch of Deadpool & Wolverine

Then, there are the incursions. Admittedly, Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness' post-credits scene isn't all that memorable. Not yet, anyway. Charlize Theron's Clea showing up to tell Doctor Strange he needs to clean up some cosmic mess, though, at least allows Marvel Studios to retroactively act like incursions were present throughout the past half-decade's stories. The literal collision of universes is a big deal, with the Russos even describing it as a "profound" devastating event. Much like Scarlet Witch's arc and return, it's a neat piece of tidying-up for something that otherwise rang hollow.

As the joke goes, Kevin Feige can look you dead in the eye and tell you something was always the plan, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary. That has never been more obvious – and better implemented – than in the connective tissue between Multiverse of Madness and Avengers: Doomsday.

Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness is available to stream now on Disney Plus, ahead of the release of Avengers: Doomsday on December 18 in the US and 16 in the UK.

Look ahead with our list of upcoming Marvel movies and check out how to watch the Marvel movies in order ahead of your next rewatch. See you next week as we revisit Thunderbolts.

I'm the Senior Entertainment Writer here at GamesRadar+, focusing on news, features, and interviews with some of the biggest names in film and TV. On-site, you'll find me marveling at Marvel and providing analysis and room temperature takes on the newest films, Star Wars and, of course, anime. Outside of GR, I love getting lost in a good 100-hour JRPG, Warzone, and kicking back on the (virtual) field with Football Manager. My work has also been featured in OPM, FourFourTwo, and Game Revolution.

#3912. Archetype go all in on the Mass Effect vibes with a FemJun reveal, but I'm just left hoping they'll call the alternative option MascJun to balance it out

I know it, you know it, hell, I'm sure developer Archetype Entertainment know it: Exodus is kind of just Mass Effect again. That's in part because the DNA of the game has been built by series vets like Drew Karpyshyn, Chad Robertson and James Ohlen. But it's also because, well, they're putting FemShep in the game. Yes, I'm being a tad facetious here, but when the latest trailer for your game is literally titled "Female Jun Reveal," well, comparisons will be made!

To top it all off, a blog post from the devs literally refers to the alternate gender for the protag as FemJun. They know what they're doing. In any case, first up, her voice actor! She's being played by Carina Conti, an up and comer last digitally heard in Mafia: The Old Country as Isabella Torrisi. Male Jun (who hasn't been given a nickname, which couldn't possibly serve to other female Jun (and MascJun is right there!)) has also had his voice actor confirmed as Stephen Oyoung, who you'll have heard as Mister Negative in Insomniac's Spider-Man games and Red Hood in Gotham Knights.

It's been previously confirmed that no matter which gender you pick for Jun, you'll be able to romance whoever you like, so, happy smoochin'! The story will stay the same too, as will dialogue options, though I'm imagine some pronoun switcheroos will take place somewhere along the line.

I'm mostly just left feeling that this doesn't really seem like it'll fix the game's boring hero problem. Edwin made note of Jun's quite lacklustre vibe earlier this year, aptly tearing down MascJun's Instagram visage, though this was prior to the face model and voice actor change the character has undergone. Personally, I'm not sure that'll be enough, and FemJun kind of matches that Instagram look; the perfect bun and bangs that pop out when she takes her helmet off is quite silly too. Ah well! A game isn't done until it's done (which, in theory, will be April 7th next year).

#3911. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (28th November)

Hello chums, well done for making it through another week.

It's been a bit of a quiet one here, overall. The biggest news was arguably the addition of a new GameCube game to the NSO library along with a new feature that finally lets you get rid of that awful border pattern.

Elsewhere though, we received the release date for Silksong's upcoming DLC, and it's really not far off. Plus, Nintendo revealed its new Winter merch range in Japan, and we're desperately hoping it also comes to the UK.

Opinion After Finishing Ocarina Of Time, I'm Left Jonesing For A Proper Sequel

Review Gamesir Nova Vision Controller For Switch 1 & 2 - Unique Features Elevate This Mid-Range Pad

It's all Denshattack! this weekend as I squeeze in an indie before GOTY season is in full swing. And I'm loving it. It's a celebration of counterculture and a love letter to the Dreamcast's era of excess. I'm not very good at it, but practice makes perfect.

I'm probably the only person here to not have played Ocarina of Time’s remake yet, but that's next as my early holiday game. And I do have a Fortune's Weave playthrough to continue, but at this point I'm just going to wait on all the DLC to release.

I’m doing a wee bit of travelling this weekend so I’ve brought my trusty Switch 2 along to keep me company. I still have a few games to catch up on including some I’ve said I’d play in previous WAYP entries but (unsurprisingly) not got around to them just yet.

I’ve been in a bit of Pokémon mood (as I write this on the train with my Pikachu suitcase) so it’s only right I progress more in Legends Z-A as I dropped it last year. I also picked up Bravely Default: Flying Fairy HD Remaster (at a bargain) the other week with much encouragement from my friends Joe and….well another Joe, so I also have that to try. I’ve always wanted to play the series so I’m pretty excited!

Made it to mission 83 in Earth Defense Force 5 and things went Pacific Rim after being teased from the very start of the game. I do wonder how many more missions are left... Water temple done in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a much more manageable affair then in the original format. I am beginning to understand why people don’t want the game to end. Gotta go update Mario Kart World and check the new tracks. Despite its stubborn absence on Switch, I was sent a review code for the STEAM version of Shoresy: Legends of the North to mess with so I will be spending the weekend with it while giving Tape to Tape a much deserved rest on the bench. While on the PC topic, I need to get things ready for early-access Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV. Game of the week is Goodboy Galaxy! I finally have the physical edition on Switch and I’m quite looking forward for some GBA related antics. Pretty sure this was not supposed to be played on my giant TV screen, but nowadays my eyes can hardly deal with the original GBA tiny screen. Lets hope Santa brings me new glasses.

This weekend is the last we’ll have before Christmas to get the decorations up. Experience tells me that what should take one morning will end up stretching across the entire weekend, so the chances of slipping in some gaming are slim.

We’ve finished Ocarina now, so I’m currently splitting my evenings between the Isle of Neasied, Leonida, and a dozen other places. GOTY is coming! Have a good one, folks.

I am right at the very end of Pragmata and I’m ready for a big sob. If it’s all heading in the direction I think it is, I have just one battle left then we’re done. It might not run the best on Switch 2, but man, what a great little game! More of this please, Capcom! After that, I think I’ll finally get round to The Seance of Blake Manor. A couple of weeks should be enough time to polish it off before Silksong returns to gobble up all my time, right?

Those are our plans, but what about yours? Let us know what you'll be slapping in your Switch (2) in the poll below.

Finished Ocarina last week after stretching it out a bit. It was stretched out because I got into Ember Knights and ended up mixing that in with Ocarina. I bought Ember Knights over a year ago for the co-op play, but the friend and I that tried it then didn’t really get into it. This time I have gotten into it solo and have been playing quite a bit.

I am enjoying it more now because some things “clicked” for me recently about how combat works in action games. A year ago I played about 45 hours of Street Fighter 6 which is the first fighting game I ever played. In the past I didn’t have any terminology for thinking about the combat in action games, but having played a fighting game gave me that terminology and that has helped me enjoy combat in games so much more.

I played and loved games like Hollow Knight, Silksong, and Hades in the past, but it was a lot of memorization. Now, by thinking about startup/active/recovery frames I am able to more quickly find my openings. This also clicked for me while playing Ocarina. In the past, when I played it I didn’t really understand the fights that are very much structured around these ideas. I guess back then I probably muddled through and traded hits and used a lot of fairies, I don’t clearly remember. I have to revisit the combat in BOTW and TOTK sometime with these ideas in mind as well.

Continuing with the combat theme I started Fountains which I bought on GOG. I still need to get to a successful run in Ember Knights (I’ve been to the last world the last couple runs).

Someday I need to replay Tunic because I bet not having these ideas is why the combat in that game seemed so difficult to me.

The answer is Grand Theft Auto 6, of course. I’m halfway through chapter two. In my humble opinion, Rockstar has once again created a masterclass open world game, arguably the greatest of all time.

I’ve been thinking about all the things Rockstar manages to do that makes their games feel special. For starters, the amount of money and resources at their disposal helps build the scope they are aiming for. And secondly, there is a singular word that defines their ambition: moments. Simply put, they understand how to create interesting moments throughout the entirety of their games (RDR2 is a great example) that not only feel unique, but personal, as if they were put into place at a specific time just for you to encounter and maybe nobody else.

Interestingly, I love the game but I don’t spend much time playing. It’s such a dense game that I want to take my sweet time with it, and experience what each town and county has to offer. I don’t care if it will take months to beat the game—because the entire game is another Rockstar “moment”.

One of these moments occurred when I was dirt biking up in the hills. I heard commotion off the beaten path so I go explore the noises. There were two friends hunting. One guy is dressed up in a deer outfit, and his buddy “accidentally” shot him. They ask me to grab their truck and take them the hospital. On the way the two start arguing in the backseat, with the guy who got shot saying it was done on purpose because he slept with his wife. All hell broke loose, and they were fighting over the shotgun. The guy who originally got shot ended up blowing the head off his friend during the struggle, and pushed him out of the car. I finish the drive to the hospital and the man thanks me, giving me his shotgun as a thank you gift.

In another incident, I’m cruising the backroads with Lucia when she notices three people on a bridge. Two of the guys are tempting the other to jump off into the water. #3910. PS Plus Essential's Next Update Looks a Bit Better in Japan Than the Rest of the World

It’s all subjective, of course, but Japan’s PS Plus Essential update for December 2026 looks a little bit better than what we’re getting in the west.

Now if we’re looking at pure value here, the Japanese lineup is objectively better: the Bleach game retails for $59.99, while Amnesia is $24.99. The former is also available on PS5 and PS4, whereas the latter is only available for PS4 (although you can of course play it on PS5 via backwards compatibility).

Bleach is also newer, having released in 2025, while Amnesia is from 2023.

But it does ultimately all come down to taste, I suppose; survival horror fans may be much happier with Frictional’s title – especially if they have no real interest in anime. I suppose the lineup in Japan does lack variety, as you’re getting two very similar titles from Bandai Namco there.

Amnesia: The Bunker did release in Japan, so I’m not entirely sure why the lineup is different between regions.

Sony is putting a lot of marketing into its domestic region at the moment, as it tries to reverse its flagging fortunes. It’s also just launched a new PS Portal there, and is putting a pretty big promotional campaign behind it. Maybe it thinks this lineup will be more enticing to Japanese players.

Interesting stuff, though, which selection would you have preferred? I’ve had the Bleach game on my wishlist for a little while, so I think I would have rather got that – but I can certainly see why people would prefer the more varied worldwide selection as well.

#3909. Mondrayn is a putrid, crunchy pixel art RPG about escaping from limbo where "dying doesn't mean the end of your suffering"

Everything's a bit grim these days, so let's just go all in on the misery shall we? Let's start with this line from the game's Steam page we'll be talking about today: "Mondrayn is a grim JRPG with survival elements where dying doesn't mean the end of your suffering." Crikey! You're telling me the sweet release of death won't be so saccharine after all? Sounds rough, so it's a good thing Mondrayn looks so darn compelling.

The world of Mondrayn is a dead one. You start out waking up in a city, it's in a gnarly state, of course, overrun by a disease of unknown origin. Horrible monsters are roaming about the place, cults are performing nasty rituals, and you've got no memories, so all you can do is try and make any friends you can, kill the undead and get out of, all places, limbo.

Mondrayn is an RPG in the sense that it utilises turn-based combat, "intertwined with shootouts." I'm not entirely sure how that manifests, you do seem to be able to do both regular attacks and special moves, the state of characters seems to have an impact, but truthfully I don't mind not understanding because what I'm here for are the utterly, delectably rancid vibes on display.

Every single pixel in this game looks like it was dipped in a vat of grime, puss, blood and vomit, and I revel in it! The enemy portraits are crunchy and violet, they look ripped straight out of some obscure art book for a Warhammer-esque tabletop game no one has ever heard of. It looks a bit fantasy, a bit steampunk, and incredibly, incredibly grimdark. It's the kind of world I'd rather instantly top myself than spend a second longer in, so, kudos to the fictional characters in it that have no choice in the matter for managing better than me. As it stands, Mondrayn has no release date, but you can wishlist it on Steam in the meantime.

The GTA 6 pool boy scene in the Safe Word mission sees Jason trapped on the set of a porno after accidentally taking on a new cover story as one of the stars of the show. Initially, Lucia finds this all very funny before it starts to get serious, forcing Jason to make a choice as to how far he'll go to avoid blowing his cover. Of course, it's actually you making this GTA 6 choice, and the reality is that it's nowhere near as impactful as it seems. So, having tested both options, here are all the outcomes to the pool boy scene in Grand Theft Auto 6.

The short answer is that your decision to participate or not in the pool boy scene doesn't really matter as the effects of either choice have a tiny impact:

Choosing not to participate is obviously the better option if you're trying to maintain a good GTA 6 relationship status with Lucia. And even if you do choose to participate, the negative impact on the relationship isn't significant enough to cause a substantial drop in its level – Jason and Lucia's relationship stayed at the maximum Hot Together level for me when trying out both decisions.

Otherwise, the rest of the Safe Word mission plays out the same. Immediately after you make your choice, Lucia sets off a car alarm to interrupt filming, giving Jason a chance to slip away and infiltrate Gil's office to find his vault. There are a few things you can interact with in here but none of them have any effect either besides the remote, which is necessary for revealing the vault and progressing the mission to the final stage.

#3906. The siren call of user-generated content has caught Dead by Daylight in its snare, as Behaviour Interactive outline a big revamp update slated for next year

Weather, new models, better maps, it'll have it all

The promise of user-generated content, this idea that you could host a platform that grows infinitely because the people that interact with it make things for it and you don't even have to pay anyone, is an alluring one. And its siren call has come for Dead by Daylight, as developer Behaviour Interactive have outlined the future of the game, which includes a way to make your own bits for the multiplayer horror game.

"What if you could create your own Dead by Daylight experiences?" explains a blog post recapping the plans for how the game is going to change. "As one of the most exciting updates coming in 2027, the Dead by Daylight Workshop will open the doors to user-created content in some incredible ways. From designing your own Maps and importing custom assets, to modifying game rules, objectives, and even creating entirely new modes, the possibilities are vast."

The post goes on to note that anything created in the workshop will "exist separately from all our classic modes, with dedicated creation tools and moderation provided to ensure experienced modders have everything they need to do their best work, and all submissions meet our official guidelines." I am always hesitant when it comes to UGC faff, because the ability to make your own custom Debbie Daylight maps might sound promising, but people do actually have to engage with them for the whole thing to work. It's just putting a hat on a hat!

Anyway, the workshop isn't the only thing Behaviour have in the works. For one, the game is getting a big visual overhaul. You can expect lighting improvements, more detailed assets and "tons of atmospheric touches," alongside revamps of particular maps like the Temple of Purgation and Backwater Swamp. Killers and survivors will be getting some TLC too by "improving character textures, proportions, hair, and animations to make them look and feel more lifelike. That includes updated character rigs, new motion capture, and new facial animation technology designed to better express a character’s fear, pain, and struggles over the course of a Trial."

Beyond all of that, a dynamic weather system is coming to the game, meaning you'll now have to deal with the likes of rain, thunderstorms, snow and heavy wind, all of which can impact matches. Onboarding for newer folks should be getting some improvements too, with the addition of a "more cinematic introduction, clearer explanations and tutorials of game mechanics, and a more gradual introduction," to the game. All of this will be coming in one big update sometime in 2027, so, keep your eyes peeled for whenever that drops.

#3905. The Witcher 3 Remastered Patch 5.02 Fixes Annoying PS5 Stutters, Improves Performance, and Much More

The Witcher 3 Remastered has a new update on PS5, and it's available to download right now, weighing in at a reasonable 1.6GB.

Patch 5.02 is the one many have been waiting for, as it addresses the game's most annoying technical issue on console. I am, of course, referring to the momentary stutters that occurred when autosave was triggered.

This problem was especially noticeable when quest information popped up on the screen, both when you began a quest and finished it. Thankfully, CD Projekt Red's finally taken action.

The patch also improves v-sync and VRR "behaviour" on PS5, which should result in a smoother overall experience. Screen flickering has also been addressed.

On top of those more-than-welcome adjustments, the update is packed with bug fixes — some of which are related to the remaster's new lighting techniques, which could result in some areas looking poorly or incorrectly illuminated.

And in terms of gameplay, we're looking at a bunch of balancing tweaks to a number of Geralt's skills. Some of these perks simply weren't being calculated properly, so you should be more effective in combat right out of the gate with this update installed.

#3904. Opinion: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Is Still Nintendo's Best Credits Sequence

Editor's note: It really should go without saying...so we're not going to say it. Common sense is your friend, as always.

Like many people, I replayed the N64 Ocarina of Time before diving into the Switch 2 remake. This is a game that I have played from start to finish perhaps more than any other, but there were still things on this return visit that I had half-forgotten: my love for the Fire Temple, the unexpected emotion of the Twinrova death, the Nabooru Iron Knuckle reveal.

Chief among them was the sublime credits sequence. I had forgotten how much it slaps.

I took my time with the Switch 2 remake, mopping up side quests and collectibles before heading to the grand finale, but the entire time I was wondering whether Nintendo would remain faithful to the post-game scenes that roll behind the reams of staff names.

Unsurprisingly, the end result is as faithful as they come. I sobbed as I watched these scenes I've already seen so many times play in gorgeous 4K, and it convinced me that, yes, this is still an all-timer.

My tears started right from the jump. Is anyone else always caught a little off guard by how quickly that final cutscene ends? Zelda promises to send Link back, she plays the ocarina, and then boom, credits. Come on, Nintendo, I'm an emotional wreck here!

We begin with a somewhat standard affair, panning shots of the locales you've spent the last 30+ hours getting (re)acquainted with while the most delicious rendition of Zelda's Lullaby plays in the background. It's a reminder that these places are now safe because of you. Hyrule is finally at peace. But... where are all the people?

A fade to black is broken by the sound of the Lost Woods theme and the most joyous sight in all of gaming: every NPC from the game enjoying a boogie together at Lon Lon Ranch.

Malon and Ingo grin in each other's arms. The Music Box man is happily being twirled around by a bunch of Kokiri (who "can't leave the forest" unless there's a shindig, apparently). Talon and the Carpenters sing a melody together around the fire. Forget the places; these are the people that you have saved by defeating Ganon. Hyrule is a better place thanks to you, and their smiles show it.

It's just as things hit their most optimistic that Nintendo delivers the killer blow. The music fades as we pan to Mido and King Zora. They're not singing and dancing around the fire with the rest, but sitting at the edge of the ranch, solemnly looking at the floor.

Oh god. We didn't make everyone's lives better. For these two, we awakened the sages of the Forest and Water Temples, and took away their loved ones in the process. It's a gut punch that gets me every time.

Not as much as the shot that follows, mind you. The twinkly Sage Chamber music enters the mix and Mido gets to his feet, pointing up at the sky as...wait for it...five Medallion-coloured lights shoot across the sky.

The lights land on Death Mountain, revealing the Sages themselves smiling down on the scene. The world is safe, and the five who helped save it still have each other. Oof.

(Side note: I've always assumed this bit a little more spiritual than the Kokiri dancing around the fire — the real Sages are still in the Chamber, and this is a bit more of a Force Ghost vibe. If they have somehow got out and that's really them, well...I hope Rauru is enjoying having all those Sage platforms to himself.)

Things wrap up with a shot of Child Link returning to his timeline, nodding self-assuredly and leaving the Master Sword in its pedestal. The music reaches its crescendo, and the credits come to a close.

But it's not over. Just like in the original game, there's a post-credit sting that sees Link return to Hyrule Castle and meet Zelda for the first time all over again. Not a word is spoken between the pair, but there's a vague sense that they both know the future they have averted. As Zelda's Lullaby plays on the ocarina once again, the scene turns sepia, and 'The End' appears.

Nintendo is no stranger to a fantastic credit sequence. We've gotten playable credit levels (recent examples like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Donkey Kong Bananza spring to mind as highlights), Smash Bros. always has some fun bonus fighting over the names, and who can forget Kirby: Planet Robobot's name-timed punching?

But none come remotely close to Ocarina for me. It's in the level of introspection that comes from the montage. Not only am I reminded of all the fun I had on the adventure, but I also get to see what all of my hard work meant for Hyrule. Zelda games are always a little cagey when it comes to letting you play around in post-Ganon Hyrule, but this more than satiates my appetite — a little 'where are they now' moment for all my favourite NPCs. The answer for them all is 'quite happy, actually.'

Having wrapped up the Switch 2 remake and watched this credit sequence roll for the Nth time in my life, I walked through to the other room where my partner was relaxing, and stood in the doorway. "Did you finish it?" she asked. I nodded. "Was it the same ending as always?" I nodded again. "Then why are you crying?"

Remember that teddy bear you were carrying around in Peaceful Rest Valley? It's in the picture. Remember how you barely survived the gold mine after fighting the five moles, and only Jeff clawed his way to safety? Ness and Paula are both dead in the photo. No other ending, in my opinion, gives the same sense of warmth, accomplishment, and closure as EarthBound, even though it does end with an ominous "The End...?" sequence that we never got to see the payoff to in the West. #3903. Slow down a bit and help a cow find a friend in the lush-looking, hand-drawn, milk deliver-em-up Milki Delivery, which is out now

I don't want to write about video games any more, I want to deliver milk in the countryside and hang out with a cow and quirky people! Sorry, what, there's a game all about that called Milki Delivery that came out today? Alright, I'll write about video games again, especially when they look as charming as this one does.

The stakes at play in Milki Delivery are very low (as are the steaks, no butchery to be found here, only one very sweet looking cow I couldn't possibly slaughter). You play as Neha, and she's made a promise to her pet cow, the titular Milki, that you'll find her a friend (I think this is a world where there aren't any cows left; yikes!). To do that, all you have to do is deliver her milk! Accept because this is an adventure game, you'll have to help out a few folks along the way.

It's a game very much about the journey, as when riding about this lush and bright countryside, you might find a group of cats that just need a little taste of that sweet creamy juice you've got. Or maybe you have some rope that a farmer needs to wrassle up some sheep. Sometimes you'll have to get a bit more involved with the various people you meet, but predominantly, you'll be delivering milk to folks who need it.

Getting around the place is quite simple too, you plot out your path ahead of time and let the game take you as it's all mouse driven. A relaxed experience to be sure, but the game's art is just so delightful to look at, I'm quite enticed by the idea of just slowing down and enjoying some pretty pictures and making friends along the way. You can make different kinds of milk, too, just be feeding Milki different ingredients. Not how that works in real life, but now I kind of wish it was.

In any case, Milki Delivery is out now, and you can pick it up on Steam.

Bucky Barnes actor Sebastian Stan has defended Thunderbolts after its weaker box office performance.

The film grossed $382 million, which, while not an outright disaster, also isn't a stellar return for Marvel.

"I think it's just when you've had a studio and you've had Marvel, and it's been so many years where they've just been knocking it out of the park, a $350 million global number just suddenly doesn't seem that much. But it's insane how much money that is, you know?" Stan said on the Next Best Picture podcast.

"So, I don't know, I still felt like for us it felt like a success," he continued. "I know a lot of care went into that and it had more nuance to it in terms of, I guess, than some of the recent ones. I don't know, from my point of view at least. Like, dealing with real issues like mental health and depression and so on. They're just a good group of people."

Stan will soon return in Avengers: Doomsday, a crossover for the ages that puts the Avengers, Thunderbolts, Fantastic Four, and the X-Men up against Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

"We love this film. We've poured a lot into it. We've had seven years to think about it. We've got Robert back, greatest actor in the world," co-director Joe Russo said recently. "I think it is unlike any movie that's been made in the Marvel universe up to this point. It's tonally very different. It's very surprising, and I think the audience is going to be very surprised when they see the movie."

Doomsday arrives this December 18. In the meantime, check out our guide to all the upcoming Marvel movies and TV shows for everything else that's on the way.

#3901. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang offers to return if that's best for the company and America, Nvidia board essentially say 'nah, we're all good'

New rulers impervious to highly persuasive message of 'come on, please give me my job back, go USA'

Nvidia's board have indicated that they aren't about to do a big u-turn and reappoint recently resigned CEO Jensen Huang, following his departure after multiple alleged instances of extramarital cavorting were reported by the press. Since his exit last week, Huang has indicated he'd be open to making such a return, were it deemed best for both the company and AMERICA.

"On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member," Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said during an investors call on November 17th (thanks, Percieving Calls Gamer). "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

That last bit seems likely to have been said with the intention of quieting down some of the speculation around a Huang return that's been bubbling away since he removed his bum from the black and green throne and that the exec embraced in a statement put out yesterday. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he wrote. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.

"Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. Nvidia is a once-in-a-generation company. If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO."

For now at least, it seems leather jacketed GPUperman will not be triumphantly flying back into his former post amid a wave of corporate and patriotic fervour. Likely as part of continued efforts to reassure moneyfolk that they won't be making negative headlines again soon following Huang's departure, Nvidia's board announced yesterday that they're establishing a "new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management". One of Huang's alleged affairs was with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The Chinese government have denied the accusations of espionage.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress is currently serving as Nvidia's interim CEO while the company's board searches for a permanent sexy leather jacket man replacement.

#3900. GTA 6 Gives PS5 a Very Rare Win Over Switch 2 in Japan

At this point, it’s well known that Switch 2 is by far the market leader in Japan.

While the PS5 still commands some marketshare, it gets dominated by the Nintendo machine on a weekly basis.

GTA 6’s launch is significant, then, because for the first time in a while it’s pushed Sony’s console in front of the Switch 2 – albeit only by a few thousand units.

According to Famitsu’s latest report, the PS5 sold 41,472 units through the week ending 22nd November, while the Switch 2 managed 36,817 units.

This is an incredibly rare scenario, and likely won’t be repeated again (if ever). But it shows that with the right software, Sony can put up a fight domestically against Nintendo.

The company’s been taking the region a lot more seriously under Japanese CEO Hideaki Nishino, launching more affordable region locked units to try and stimulate interest.

This week saw the release of the new Midnight Black model, which certainly helped contribute to the sales.

But PS5’s success was primarily motivated by GTA 6, which sold a very respectable 200,759 units at retail for the week.

That’s slightly less than GTA 5’s 304,752 units opening in 2013, although remember digital buying habits have changed dramatically in the last 13 years, and GTA 6’s physical release was not particularly compelling as it doesn’t include a disc.

A good week for Sony in its home region, then – one that’s unlikely to be replicated, but should be taken as a sign it can compete with the right lineup and pricing model.

News PS Plus Essential's Next Update Looks a Bit Better in Japan Than the Rest of the World

As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. #3899. Despite being £61.7 million in debt, bankrupt MindsEye devs Build a Rocket Boy are splurging on legal action against "a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews"

Administrators say "a substantial litigation fund is anticipated to arise"

Freshly published bankruptcy documents for perennially troubled MindsEye developer Build A Rocket Boy have spelled out the scale of the company's debt, with around £61.7 million owed to creditors. The documents also touch on founder Leslie Benzies and CEO Mark Gerhard's claims that MindsEye is the victim of an organised sabotage campaign. The company's leaders have apparently taken out even more loans in order to fund legal action against the suspected perpetrators, with the promise of a healthy payout. I'm not holding my breath.

BARB's largest debt by far is the roughly £36.5 million owed to NetEase, publishers of Marvel Rivals. Asset manager Diameter Capital Partners are the second largest external creditor, having loaned BARB around £4.25 million. A further $19 million is owed to "group undertakings" – "group undertakings" meaning debts to parent companies, subsidiaries or fellow subsidiaries. Studio founder Benzies, meanwhile, is owed £1,158,167.05. Given that Benzies has been repeatedly accused of torpedoing MindsEye's fortunes by way of disruptive micro-management, I'm not sure many BARB staff would agree that he really deserves his million quid back at this stage, but that's what it says on paper. Smaller IOUs include £10,434.11 for Amazon Web Services, £634.36 for Unity, and a mighty £19.90 for OpenAI.

Build a Rocket Boy have been on a journey, it's fair to say. Announced in 2023, their flagship project MindsEye is a filmic GTA-ish action shooter initially billed as a full-fat demo for Everywhere, a game creation platform comparable to Roblox. MindsEye struggled to compel us before launch and did not find its people on release, with poor sales leading to layoffs even as BARB leadership insisted they could revive the game's fortunes.

The same leadership were subsequently accused by their own staff of "disastrously" mishandling the redundancies and enforcing "unbearable" crunch. Unionised BARB employees have now taken management to court for installing alleged surveillance software on their work PCs. The game's publishers Io Interactive noped out of the picture in March this year. Meanwhile, Benzies and Gerhard have thrown around accusations of a sinister espionage and sabotage campaign, carried out by unspecified perpetrators. They made a sort of revenge fantasy DLC pack about it, which our own Mark Warren characterised as we-already-have-Hitman-at-home. The bankruptcy documents shed more light on these twists and turns. According to the administrators, BARB were "funded mainly by equity investment from institutional, strategic and venture capital investors over several funding rounds, including a $110m Series D round in 2023." This followed a £32 million investment in 2020, as reported by GI. The company grew significantly during MindsEye's creation to around 500 UK and overseas employees. According to a group income statement, the company posted sequential operating losses of £47.5 million for the period ending September 30th, 2025, and £63.1 million for the year ending December 2024. The administrator proposals document also devotes some time to the aforesaid allegations of sabotage. "The directors formed the view that the game's commercial prospects may have been adversely affected by a coordinated campaign of negative online reviews and commentary," it reads. "The directors subsequently received information which they considered suggested the involvement of a number of third parties in organising and funding such activity and commenced litigation against some of those parties. The directors have indicated that such claims may be substantial in value, although the extent of any recovery remains uncertain and will be dependent upon the outcome of ongoing investigations, legal proceedings and asset recovery actions." A later section vaguely alludes to the sum BARB leadership hope to recover. "Prior to the Joint Administrators' appointment, the Company had undertaken detailed investigations and had commenced litigation against several third parties, with the assistance of the Company's former legal advisers, Brandsmiths, in connection with matters described earlier in the Proposals," the doc reads. "The Joint Administrators consider the litigation potentially to be the largest asset of the Administration." The document goes on that BARB management have "sought financial support from third party investors to fund the anticipated legal costs and expenses associated with the litigation", with some of these funding agreements already executed. "Further executed agreements and associated funding contributions are expected to be received, shortly, and a substantial litigation fund is anticipated to arise," it continues. The Joint Administrators are "currently engaging in the on-going litigation, progressing the funding arrangements entered into by the Company, and have assessed the merits of pursuing the litigation". They will liaise with relevant parties to "determine the most appropriate strategy for preserving and, where appropriate, realising value from this potential asset for the benefit of creditors and other stakeholders." The doc doesn't name who, exactly, is being taken to court. As far as I'm aware, it isn't us. Anyway, it's good to know that the company who owe over £60 million are taking on more debt in order to pursue a histrionic grievance for which they have yet to supply any real evidence whatsoever.

#3898. PC remains GTA 6's last hope for 60fps smoothness as Rockstar confirm such an option isn't coming to even the swankiest consoles

Poor little game boxes just can't handle it

As you've probably heard, GTA 6 is out on consoles this week and targeting 30 FPS on that hardware. Despite reports claiming one may not be far away, there's still no official word on a PC port, hence why we've not got a review that delves deep into analysis of just how central to the experience the smell reaction system is.

The wait for confirmation of a PC version continues, then, and it looks like that might well be the only chance people get to play the crime sandbox at 60fps, with Rockstar having confirmed that higher frame rate modes aren't en-route to even the most beefy of consoles.

Speaking to Kotaku, GTA 6's devs made clear optional 60 or 40fps performance modes aren't on the way, even for the more powerful Pro variant of the PS5.

"Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination. On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR)," Rockstar technology production director Marc Chambers put it. "The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game’s visual fidelity. While the PS5 Pro’s central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game’s complex simulation at higher frame rates."

So, there you go. The consoles just ain't got that dog in 'em. One would think, then, that being able to run GTA 6 in all its glory at higher frame rates will likely be a selling point for that PC port that's assumed to be on the way. Whether the average PC owner's graphics card and other bits will have the horses to deliver a smooth 60 is another question, and an especially pertinent one given the ongoing RAM crisis has made upgrading certain aspects of your setup ludicrously expensive.

If it requires a 5090 at a minimum, I guess those of us with less than absolute cutting edge cards will just have to keep playing Sleeping Dogs until the AI bubble bursts.

I'd never paid much mind to the Lego Minifigures Series, but the September release of the Shrek series changed all of that. One of the load-bearing icons of Zillennial culture has been Lego-ified, and I've been slowly collecting the figures ever since. I shouldn't have, though, as a Black Friday discount means I should have waited.

You can now pick up the Minifigures Shrek Series boxes for 30% off at the Lego website, so the packs are $3.49 in the US and £2.44 in the UK, and in the US the 6-pack box is also down to $20. With 12 figures to collect, a 30% saving gets you 12 boxes for the price of 9 (although Minifigures are random, and by the way my own collection is going, I'm going to need far more than 12 boxes to bag them all). It's certainly one of the stronger Lego Black Friday deals so far.

As far as I can tell, this is the only price reduction the Lego Minifigures Shrek Series has seen. Given that the series is due to wrap up in the next few months, it's time to start buying if you haven't already.

This six-pack doesn't actually save you money over buying six individual packs, but it's a better gift-sized pack if you're buying for someone else. And rolling six dice at once feels luckier than one die six times, right?

Don't want a minifigure, but a massive-figure? The Lego Shrek building kit, which makes a statue of Shrek and Donkey (and has a Puss in Boots minifigure) is reduced in the Black Friday sales too. It's not as cute as the figs, but it's a better build (and isn't as weird-looking as whatever we're getting in Shrek 5!).

This Shrek building kit is enjoying its first serious discount, making for a 20% saving in total. It's not a play kit but a model which you'll put on a shelf or cupboard. Not all brands are reducing this kit just yet, and Amazon has one of the few reductions.

When the Lego Minifigures Shrek series was announced, I knew I could very quickly spend too much money on these boxes. For those who aren't familiar, there are 12 figures to collect, and each box has a random one — statistically, you're likely to need to buy more than 12 boxes to get them all.

So far I've opened six boxes: I've gotten the Fiona and Donkey combo, Prince Charming... and two Merlins and two Fairy Godmothers. Luck isn't with me, but I'm holding out for a hero. I don't need every model (and I really don't need another Merlin or Fairy Godmother...), but I'd love to get Shrek, and maybe Lord Farquaad and Gingie, so I've collected all the main characters.

To pace buying them, I set myself a list of 12 minor life goals to achieve; each time I hit one, I get a box. They're nothing major: milestones in my marathon training plan, targets in my creative hobbies, a few easy wins like my birthday and Christmas. And my flatmate gifted me a box too.

I'm no Minifigures Series analyst, but I'm under the impression that Lego will stop selling these kits in January, when the next range seems due to release. According to rumors, this is set to be a Castles themed range; my bank account is glad that it's not from another pop culture franchise I like like Lord of The Rings, AKA some of the best Lego sets. But that means that there's not long to go for me to buy these kits.

That's why I'm jumping on this deal; it could be my last hurrah to get Shrek himself. And yes, I've identified several goals which could be achieved in the next few weeks, so I'll earn everything I buy in the deals (well, as long as I can motivate myself for a cold December 30km run...)

The only problem now is that Lego's website has a maximum limit of 5 Minifigures sets where I live (it's at 24 in the US, you lucky things) which won't take me to the minimum spend for free delivery. So I guess I'll have to find something else to order too...

This is just the start: we've rounded up all the best Black Friday Lego deals you should know about, as well as all of the other Black Friday toy deals.

#3896. Hitman, 007 First Light PS5 Crossover Makes Lenny Kravitz Your New Ally

It's a bit surprising this crossover hasn't already happened, to be honest, given IO Interactive is the studio behind both of the games, but it's now been confirmed a Hitman and 007 First Light collaboration is happening.

The content is live from today until 24th December 2026, and it takes the form of a new Elusive Target in Hitman. Lenny Kravitz, who is playing Bawma from 007 First Light, is the next celebrity to feature in Hitman, but this time, he's on Agent 47's side.

Bawma has been betrayed by three of his associates, and he's called in the bald assassin to take them down.

Up for elimination are Horace Stockton, Oswald Spoon, and Zui.

The new set of Elusive Targets and the mission hosting them brings with it the likeness and voice of Lenny Kravitz, who you'll hear from throughout the level via Agent 47's earpiece.

"Bawma is such a fun and interesting character to portray, so I was excited to step back into a new world with him for 007 First Light," said Kravitz. "Seeing Bawma team up with Agent 47 is something I think fans of both games are going to love."

The mission will be available until 24th December, but if you own a copy of the game, then you'll retain permanent access to the Arcade version of it. It can also be accessed free of charge for those who don't have Hitman 3, as it's being added to the demo of the game.
