Former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser has posted an apology to the "haters" after sharing some AI slop to celebrate Thanksgiving.

The ex-president shared a post featuring himself at a Thanksgiving table with Bowser and Donkey Kong, with all the telltale signs of AI artwork – namely, it looking terrible – but quickly deleted the post following blowback.

In a post on Twitter, Bowser responds to the reaction, saying, "Apologies if I offended people with my AI generated post. It was sent to me by a friend and it made me smile." He then addresses the "haters," saying "the message remains the same – I wish you a Happy Thanksgiving."

While it could've been an innocent bit of unc posting that you might see from your relatives on Facebook, people have been more annoyed by Bowser's somewhat dismissive attitude towards the responses urging him to not to promote usage of the slop machine and instead work with actual artists.

Others have been expressing disappointment that the former president of a company that values creativity as much as Nintendo would use AI artwork. One response says, "You were the CEO of the American branch of one of the most art focused triple a video game studios," calling the post and response "tone deaf."

Another points out the apology's wording, saying, "Calling people who simply called out the fact that you used ai 'haters' is not the mature look you're going for, Doug."

Bowser took on the role of Nintendo of America president following Reggie Fils-Aimé retiring from the role in 2019. He then led Nintendo through the majority of the Switch era, before stepping down from the role in 2025. Devon Pritchard was named as his successor and currently serves as the president of Nintendo of America.

#3865. GTA 6 players are being abducted by aliens and knocked out by Bigfoot

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only been out for a matter of hours, and players have already tracked down a UFO in the woods and a Bigfoot in the swamps.

The UFO encounter is a random night-time event in Kelly County, on a dirt road near the Starlet Motel safehouse east of Port Gellhorn. You'll need to have finished the game's first chapter, and it's most reliable after 2am in-game.

As word spread late yesterday (18th November), it seems the event will kick off if you find a car at the side of the road with its headlights flickering, its trunk open, and clothes strewn around it. Follow the trail into the trees towards a blue glow, and you'll catch a UFO beaming down on a woman before it drops her and flies off. Head back to her car, as she requests, and the UFO returns for you. You apparently black out and come round three days later, and a bronze trophy called The Truth Is Out There should unlock.

You can seemingly trigger the event as either Jason or Lucia, and it isn't needed for 100 percent completion.

And that's not the only close encounter you can expect, either. YouTuber Lazarbeam bumped into Bigfoot on the afternoon of 18th November, hours before the game launched in the UK, while one Reddit user reported that they weren't quite sure what they'd stumbled on, titling their post "I think I found Bigfoot".

Leonida's version of Bigfoot is actually the Skunk Ape, Florida's own swamp cryptid, and it can be found in the swamplands near Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County as soon as free roam opens up. Listen out for a loud roar, then use Jason's tracking ability to follow it through the swamp. You may find it feeding on a deer carcass, while a second sighting has been reported south of Watson Bay.

Either way, the trail seemingly ends at a strange, human-like tree. Investigate it, and Jason blacks out, triggering a short cutscene in which the creature creeps up on him, as shown in this video. He later wakes near his vehicle, drenched in sweat. Save your ammo, though, as shooting at it won't do you any good.

Cryptids and aliens are, of course, something of a Rockstar tradition by this point. GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery kept players hunting for years, and Output Lag has already spotted two NPCs in a GTA 6 bar talking about goings-on there. Nobody has cracked a full Chiliad-style puzzle in the new game yet, but I'm sure that's just a matter of when, not if.

GTA 6 launched today on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, although some have been getting in on the action earlier as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3864. GTA 6's Car Physics Were Tuned by a Gran Turismo Pro

Rockstar hired a former Gran Turismo pro to help master the car handling in GTA 6.

Lewis Bentley, a 2018 GT World Series Finalist, says he spent the last three-and-a-half years with the studio’s physics team, working on how the cars feel to drive.

In a now-deleted YouTube video – watched by GT Planet – he says he helped “put the auto in Grand Theft Auto”. He’s credited as a developer on the Physics Development Group, and he said in his video that the entire team was “amazing”.

The Edinburgh-based dev is no stranger to real-life racing, as it fielded its own winning team in the 24 Hours of Nürburgring event four years ago. Ben Lyons, who made up part of the squad, was the Technical Director in charge of physics on the title.

I personally really love the way cars feel in the game.

Each type has its own distinctive handling model, and you can really feel the difference when you go to a Mod Shop and tune your car to taste.

It doesn’t have the distinctive heavy handling of GTA 4, but it’s also not quite as arcadey as GTA 5 either – I’d say it sits somewhere comfortably between the two, which is a good place to be.

I love all the extra work that’s been put into the DualSense’s haptic feedback, too; the way you can physically feel the change of grip between the different road surfaces – it’s impressive stuff.

I just wish Rockstar had put a little more energy into the races themselves, because they do rely on aggressive rubber banding, which is pretty frustrating. Considering how meticulously the rest of the game is crafted, it would have been nice if a bit more thought went into this aspect.

All in all, though, I’m not surprised to learn GTA 6 had real-life race car drivers and pro Gran Turismo players on its team. You spend a good chunk of your time in Leonida driving, and I think by and large Rockstar really nailed this important aspect of the game.

#3863. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

That means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

For what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

Indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

However, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint issue in bright ambient light.

If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

The long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The big brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

#3862. World of Warcraft: Forever has more weekly players than WoW has seen in 15 years, says Blizzard

World of Warcraft: Forever now has more people playing each week than World of Warcraft has seen in 15 years, according to Blizzard.

"Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years!" executive producer and World of Warcraft vice president Holly Longdale posted. "Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever!"

Longdale was quoting a post from the official World of Warcraft account, which shared a batch of "By the Numbers" stats for the new edition.

Since it launched on 4th November, players have created 15,160,147 characters and 140,764 guilds, completed 1,480,343,357 quests, and defeated 9,786,925,806 enemies.

Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years! Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever! 💙♾️ https://t.co/bMLQduLri2

They've also formed 71,309,889 parties, used 28,696,386 camping items, and there have been 28,938,569 PvP kills.

Collectively, we've died a lot, too - 196,851,761 times in total, with Archmage Arugal, the final boss of Shadowfang Keep, seemingly the deadliest boss.

"You're breaking records by the day!" the post read.

Earlier this month, Blizzard said WoW: Forever was the biggest launch in World of Warcraft history by peak concurrent players, and that it had brought in the highest number of returning players the game has ever seen.

Longdale added at the time that it had pulled in the most new players for a WoW launch in 15 years. It has since suffered its first controversy, though, with a now-fixed gold exploit.

Last week, players pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. At the time of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

The game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among new and returning players.

#3861. Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

You lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

The game's New York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

Back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's New York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Opening a GTA 6 bank vault is one of the best ways to make off with a big score during a robbery, with potentially $100,000 or more in bills and valuables from a single heist.

But those huge bank vault doors are completely impenetrable, and confusingly, even after you've learned how to drill into a vault as part of a Chapter 3 story mission, you still won't be able to open vault doors in open world bank robberies.

Here's the trick: you've got to get someone to open bank vault doors for you. Only then can you steal all that sweet cash.

Your GTA 6 fence, Yasmani, will begin offering you tips once you start selling him stolen goods in Chapter 3: jewelry store heists targeting specific items and which ATM jobs have the most cash, for example. These are worth doing anyway as they get you the snap gun.

If you complete every job Yasmani has and keep asking for more, he'll also offer you a tip for $10,000 in Chapter 4. Pay it, and he'll give you the locations of two security vans (armored cars) in Vice City. They'll show up on your map as pink icons.

Towards the end of Chapter 4, after the main heist, if you haven't completed every job for Yasmani, you'll get the "That's Where the Money Is" opportunity to tail an armored car to a bank vault.

There are multiple banks with vaults that armored cars visit. While driving around the areas near these banks and keeping your eyes peeled, you may spot an armored car without Yasmani's tip. It could take quite a while, though!

You can see which banks have vaults by looking under "Big Bank Jobs" in the "Robberies" category on your map. There are four big banks in Ocean Beach, two downtown, one in Tequesta, and one at Vice City International Airport.

Follow the armored car until it parks outside a bank, though make sure to keep your distance as otherwise he won't park. Watch as one of the drivers gets out and walks into the bank. You can follow him to see where he goes, though bank layouts differ and he may take different routes. He may walk through the front doors, or he may go in a side entrance or a roll-up door in the back.

Once he's all the way inside—not just inside the front doors, but deep into the bank—he'll head to the vault and open it.

You can't open that vault yourself! Only the armored car driver can. That's the trick.

Once the guard is in the back of the bank, begin the robbery. Search for the vault in the back. You may need to use explosives to open the door the guard went through, or you can look for a door you can open with the snap gun. You'll find the vault door open with the armored car driver nearby. Subdue him and grab all the cash off the cart inside the vault.

There are several safe deposit boxes in the vault you can open for extra loot. Use your focus ability to highlight which boxes you can loot, and shoot them to open them up. You can also blow open all the boxes at once using a grenade or sticky bomb. Grab the loot from each.

If you really want to clean the place out, there's still all the cash drawers in the front of the bank and a small safe, or multiple safes, somewhere else, usually in an office in the back. You can open these standard safes with safe codes.

The armored car parked outside has loot in it, too. The thing is, it may despawn while you're inside the bank. If you want to loot it, place a sticky explosive on the rear door, which won't let the truck despawn. (Be stealthy: there's another guard still watching the truck). When you leave the bank after the robbery, detonate the bomb and grab the loot.

The best way to enter a bank is through a back door, if the building has one, (using the snap gun to avoid alarms) or a roll-up door. If the guard you're following goes in the back, he may leave the doors unlocked behind him, and you may not even have to unlock any doors at all to reach the vault. Just be prepared to run into multiple security guards and employees you'll need to subdue.

You will want both Jason and Lucia along for any bank vault jobs you pull. There is so much cash and valuables to grab you'll easily fill up four bags, which requires two people to carry. (You can hand loot bags to your partner by interacting with them and choosing the "Hand over bag" prompt). You'll also want one character to work as crowd control while you're looting the bank.

A silenced gun is a good idea: you want to delay setting off alarms for as long as possible, and if bank employees or citizens hear gunshots they may panic and trigger the alarm, or flee from the bank and call the cops.

In a lot of robberies you can find the security footage and destroy it while the robbery is in progress. Big banks have cloud-based cameras which won't allow you to destroy the footage. Keep a lookout (using focus) for cameras and shoot them out (with silenced pistols) as quickly as you can.

If an alarm goes off during a vault robbery, you'll get an instant four-star wanted level, which means SWAT trucks, roadblocks, and helicopters. Park your car in a good spot outside so you can jump into it easily, and have some idea of where you want to drive to during your escape.

#3859. Infamous GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek is back, and this time the group claims to have leaked a full development build of the game

CyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game launched, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site. This new leak appears to be making good on a threat posted back in October, where the group stated its intent to release a full, playable build of the game.

Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB. Eurogamer has seen the site and can confirm this is what the group has claimed, however I have been unable to verify the existence of any actual files. On the site, CyberLeek claims this build is from November 2026 - meaning it is very close to (if not the actual) release build. The 'executable file appears to be missing from the build, however, meaning you cannot actually - yet - get it up and running. CyberLeek is threatening to release this file at a later date, however.

"It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads. "[Cyberleek] holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto 6, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one. The main executable is held on a countdown." CyberLeek says the executable will be released earlier than planned if its crypto token reaches a predetermined value. Many of the leaks to date have been related to a CyberLeek crypto scheme. Previously, it was estimated that the group cashed out at least £200,000.

What does all this mean? There's a very realistic chance that the game could be up and running on PC soon - undercutting Rockstar's unannounced PC release by a matter of months, if current rumours are to be believed. "This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps," the statement continues. "[CyberLeek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons.

"If the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds, [CyberLeek] will work to get a PS5 build - a fallback, most likely never required. Either way: the Xbox build is going out. No double dipping for Take-Two/Rockstar." It seems these are not empty threats.

CyberLeek has been a thorn in Rockstar's side for a while now. The group initially claimed it took this action in the name of "Gamers' Rights", supposedly fighting for consumers in relation to the controversial discontinuation of game-discs and the digital-only future being pursued by game publishers. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity.

#3858. Fish with a sniper rifle takes aim at Tim Sweeney's hopes and dreams, as genAI-free meme game tops Epic Games' vibe-coding megajam

Epic Games are, as you're probably aware, going big on genAI at the moment. To the extent that, last month, the Tim Sweeney-helmed company announced the Epic AI MegaJam. Build a playable game in Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite with help from as many AI agents or tools as you like was the pitch.

So, naturally, sorting the submissions by 'Popular' turns up a game about a fish with a sniper rifle whose creator says they deliberately made it without using any generative AI.

The game's called LSD:FIH and sees a cigarette-smoking bit of shoe-wearing marine life go full MLG and start pulling off trickshots on blobs. If you struggled to parse that, you'll probably struggle even more with developer PolyCube's description of it as being a "computer game about a fih aura-farming". "No AI was used to make this game," is the other line in their description, which is far easier to parse.

"I made a game for the Epic's 'vibe-coding gamejam' megajam without using any AI in four days," they expanded on not Bluesky. "Sorta ran out of time so gameplay didn't turn out how I wanted, but hey it's still pretty aura."

Other submissions the megajam included a game called THIS GAME IS AI SLOP and one dubbed Goon Patrol - Director's Cut. If you're wondering how a game without genAI use could be allowed to stand among the slop masterpieces, it's because Epic ended up having to make clearer not long after the jam was announced that submissions didn't have to make use of genAI as a hard rule, leaving it up to the developer how much or little was worked in.

Still, I imagine noted genAI advocate Tim Sweeney's not best pleased that a game deliberately swimming against the slop tide shows up at the top if you hit up the Popular filter. Then again, he's been very busy posting important things about the situation with Jensen Huang and Nvidia lately, so maybe he hasn't noticed.

Yes, the last post I've linked there is the Sweens giggling at an AI image of him, Huang, Johan Andersson, and John Carmack as the heads carved into Mount Rushmore that he himself asked Grok to generate. As you do.

#3856. Where to buy a PS5 and PS5 Pro LIVE: Stock is running low this weekend but there are discounts if you know where to look

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a bizarre blast from the past, PS5 stock is difficult to come by right now. While I thought we were beyond the days of tracking PS5 and PS5 Pro restocks, a surge in demand from Black Friday PS5 deals (not helped by this week's Black Friday GTA 6 deals) has rendered these consoles particularly difficult to find this week.

The problem's not new either. PS5 and PS5 Pro stock has been MIA for a few months in the lead up to Rockstar's blockbuster release. While that Pro model is still absent from the shelves, though, there are ways to buy a PS5 Slim (and even save some cash) in both the US and UK right now.

PS Direct is going to be your first port of call Stateside right now. The retailer has Certified Refurbished consoles readily available on the shelves for $100 off. Meanwhile, the UK is seeing a nearly-£50 saving on a PS5 Digital Edition with GTA 6 and a DualSense included as well.

We're tracking all the latest PS5 and PS5 Pro restocks right here, so if that boosted console even looks at a virtual store shelf you'll know about it below. You'll find the web's current supply of PS5 stock right here, though, with our live updates further down the page.

I was there the first time around, tracking PS5 stock when the console first hit distribution difficulties in 2020 and then reporting on PS5 Pro restocks when the boosted console launched a few years later. Tracking consoles in the big 2026 feels like coming home, then, after years of hunting down hard-to-find gadgets like special edition releases and new Sony and Microsoft hardware.

PS Direct | Certified Refurbished for $100 off

This is my top recommendation for anyone hunting down PS5 stock on the Slim models this weekend. Sony's Certified Refurbished devices come in $100 cheaper than box-fresh consoles, and still pack everything you need in the box and a 12 month warranty. That's a Digital Edition for $499 or a Disc Edition for $549.

EE has the best PS5 bundle in the UK right now, with nearly £50 off an extra DualSense and a copy of GTA 6. The full kit would run you £519.99 for the console, £64.99 for the extra controller, and £69.99 for the latest GTA. That's £654.97 in total, while you're paying £605 today.

Going straight to the source will also secure you a PS5 at its regular selling price in the UK, though unlike the US PS Direct doesn't have any refurbished devices up for grabs here. Still, the Slim versions are available, even if the Pro's still MIA.

I wouldn't recommend this bundle over the EE option above, but if stock starts running even lower it's worth keeping as a backup. Amazon has the PS5 Disc console in stock, with an additional DualSense thrown in. However, you'll be waiting until February for shipping on this one.

It's difficult to pinpoint an exact end time to this season's PS5 stock shortages, however I'd expect things to settle down substantially in the new year. Once that holiday rush is over and GTA 6 has been in the hands of gamers for a little longer, we could see a resurgence in stock levels.

Not all inventory makes its way to the online PS5 Pro stock race, it's also worth checking in with your local stores. Sites like Best Buy and GameStop have been prioritizing in-store restocks for other hard-to-find gadgets in the last few weeks, so you never know what you might find.

PS Direct seems to be on a fairly regular PS5 Pro restock schedule in the mornings in the UK. Stock doesn't last long, but I've seen multiple reports of those listings springing to life between 6 and 8am in the last few days. It's well worth keeping an eye on, even if it does mean setting the alarm tomorrow.

Obviously I'm not recommending anyone actually check out these ludicrously inflated prices, but it just goes to show how strained things are at the moment. Stock will return in time, though, it's not worth spending more than double the asking rate of the PS5 Pro.

Stores like PS Direct and Target in particular have a restock pattern when hard-to-find gadgets run off the shelves, and many of them opt to drop new consoles earlier in the mornings. Happily for stock hunters, that's usually when competition is also at its lowest.

If you're still hunting down that golden goose it's well worth setting the alarm for your next retailer crawl.

It's not just the lack of stock at other sites, I've been shouting about Sony's Certified Refurbished consoles ever since the PS5 price jumped earlier in the year. While a disc Slim console will now set you back $649.99, Sony's renewed models cost just $549. That's with a DualSense controller and 12 month warranty included. The Digital Edition was even cheaper but has sadly been run off the shelves more recently.

PS5 Slim (Certified Refurbished) | $549 at PS Direct

GameStop has run out of PS5 Slim consoles this weekend, but it is still stocking the original "fat" model. I wouldn't take much notice of that listing, though. The store wants $639.99 for a pre-owned device - that's pretty mad considering Sony's certified refurbished (not just pre-owned) stock is available for $549.

It's business as usual for PS5 Pro stock checkers in the US. All I'm seeing this morning is inflated prices across Walmart, Best Buy, Newegg, and even GameStop's pre-owned stock. Amazon simply has an 'out of stock' message on its listing page as well.

The tale's the same across the ocean as well. Without a sniff of a PS5 Pro on the shelves there are thankfully fewer four-figure inflated rates at UK retailers, but still no stock to speak of.

Amazon was previously estimating a February shipping date for its current PS5 Slim stock, but it looks like things have shifted up the calendar. As I expected, this isn't a hard-set date but rather an indication of the retailer's low stock levels. We're now looking at January shipping for Prime members here.

For the first time all year, the PS5 Digital Edition is no longer available via Sony's Certified Refurbished scheme. This was previously my go-to method of buying a PS5 amidst the current price hikes, but with stock running dry it's back to the drawing board for now.

The Disc model is still up for grabs, though, for $549 ($100 off the new $649 MSRP).

PS5 Disc Edition (Certified Refurbished) | $549 at PS Direct

It goes without saying that, if you see an offer at a reasonable price, it's worth jumping on it as soon as possible - PS5 stock is flying off the shelves fast, so it's important not to wait too long. Otherwise, you're almost certainly going to miss out. Speed is of the essence!

Tempted by the 'offers' at Amazon and Walmart? Steel yourself, and resist - it's simply not worth grabbing PS5 consoles when they're so inflated in cost. These are being sold by cheeky third-party vendors trying to make a quick buck based on scarcity. You see, they will come back down in price eventually when more stock appears, so there's no need to waste extra cash on something like this.

Speaking of GTA, are there any accessories or extras you can grab to go alongside the console? Well, as luck would have it, we've got an entire guide dedicated to that very subject. Here are all the best Black Friday GTA 6 deals we've been able to rustle up so far!

What's the first game you're hoping to play on your new PS5? I suspect many of you are gonna say 'GTA 6,' and honestly, that's fair enough. It's an absolute phenomenon that more than lives up to the hype, and luckily, it's widely available - unlike the console to play it on.

At the moment, it feels like you're choosing between two kinds of console; the Slim Digital or the Slim Disc. As the name would suggest, one can only download digital games and doesn't have a disc drive (this is the Slim Digital). The other has a disc drive attached (the Slim Disc) so can use discs or digital downloads. This is more expensive though, so it really comes down to how you think you'll consume your games. I'd normally opt for the disc option because it provides more flexibility; you're more likely to find price cuts on physical discs at Amazon and beyond than you are digital versions, which hold their price much better.

As for the UK, it's a little more hopeful... but be warned, you will be paying a lot for the privilege. EE still has stock of the Slim digital console with GTA 6 and a bonus controller for £644.98. Meanwhile, Amazon is providing the Slim Disc console with an extra controller for £609.99. Neither is particularly cheap, but you are making some savings along the way. The one you get will depend on whether you think you'll want to get disc versions of games in the future, or if you're happy just downloading everything.

So, where can you currently buy a PlayStation 5 in the US? As of now, the only place I'm able to find it anywhere close to a reasonable price is from PlayStation Direct, where you can grab certified refurbished units. Indeed, the Slim with what looks like a disc drive is currently available there.Yes, technically PS5s are available elsewhere at stores like Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy... but they're hideously overpriced. With that in mind, I wouldn't even think about getting them. Stock will return at some point, so you're better off waiting if you can.

We're back for another day of PS5 stock-hunting, so I hope you're ready. Will it be a PlayStation 5-filled Christmas after all? Time will tell. Let's dig in, shall we?

US friends, I've just had another trawl for PS5 Pro stock and I'm coming up empty handed again. Apologies.

PlayStation Direct, GameStop, Target, Amazon, Best Buy... all absolute crickets. Well all except Walmart, which is trying to charge $1,849.99 for a PS5 Pro. Yeah, no.

I've been covering the PS5 since before it launched (and I was doing this pre-PS4 too if you must know), and the hunger for buying a PS5 feels like when the console first launched. It's pretty mad that we're back in this position. Obviously it's down to a number of factors including the launch of PS5, but there's such a scarcity of machines that it takes me right back to 2020.

Early results on the poll I posted suggest you're all here to buy a PS5 for yourself - the majority upgrading to PS5 Pro (40%) but then 30% of you are desperate to play GTA 6 and the other 30% are getting your first PS5.

There is one PS5 bundle now available at EE and it might appease those of you coming here for a way to play GTA 6 on PlayStation.

For £644.98 at EE, you can get a PS5 Slim Digital with additional DualSense controller, and a £100 EE GameCard to buy GTA 6. It's a really decent bundle as you're getting a saving of around £50 vs buying them separately.

While I continue my rounds, I'd love to know what you're here for so I can help you better!

Guys, I won't lie to you. It's not looking good.

For my UK friends, the EE PS5 GTA 6 bundle is finally out of stock, which was pretty much our last hurrah for the day as we hurtle through to 11pm.

Over the pond in the US, the PlayStation Direct Certified Refurbished Slim console with disc drive is still in stock for $549, but everyone else is outta stock or outta line with their pricings.

Before you go off galavanting across the internet in an attempt to spend your hard-earned cash on a PS5, maybe just think about what you actually need. Trust me I get it, I'm the first one to jump to the best on the market because I want the top of the range, when realistically I don't always need it.

Think about your setup? What are you plugging this PS5 into? Ideally you want a 4K OLED TV with 120Hz, HDMI 2.1, HDR10 and VRR if you're going for the Pro, otherwise you're not really taking full advantage of its features.

What's your budget? Do you really $800/£900 to spend on a console if you want the Pro?

What's most important to you? Value for money? Graphical quality? Performance? Playing physical media?

The Slim Disc edition is probably the best all-rounder, while the Digital is the most cost-effective. The Pro is for those who really do want the best looking games, without worrying too much about enhanced prices. But you think about what you need.

As we continue to search for stock, let alone any deals, it's good to make sure you know what a sensible price is for a PS5 right now, because let's face it, the internet is always eager to rip people off.

First, let's recap the actual current RRPs of the PS5 Slim, PS5 Slim Digital Edition, and PS5 Pro in the US and UK:

These are the prices that Sony upped in April 2026, so definitely bear that in mind when you're looking at deals.

Anything over $50 / £50 more than these prices right now isn't worth the spend, especially as stock is sporadically coming in at RRP or with a game or extra pad bundled for a fair price - not a complete rip off.

Sometimes it's difficult to read between the specs, but it's worth knowing what an investment in a PS5 Pro actually gets you. One of the biggest differences is the fact it comes with a 2TB internal hard drive as standard, vs the relatively measly 825GB of the OG PS5 and the 1TB PS5 Slim.

The graphics and performance are so much better too, thanks to enhanced specs and processing power, and the magic of tech like the PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, even if it does sound a bit like a superhero (although I guess it kinda is). You will absolutely need a 4K 120Hz or 144Hz TV to make the most of this though, because otherwise it's very much just wasted.

They're the two main differences really, apart from it being a much larger console - which definitely has its pros and cons when it comes to your setup solutions.

With my parting shot for the day, I just want to remind you (if needed) or state outright something you've maybe not had words to articulate: it's OK to just not buy a thing.

You don't need the PS5 Pro! No lives will be saved through your purchase of a video game console, and waiting a little bit longer for an actual deal rather than, say, going into credit card debt is probably the smart move. I don't think being frugal is an ugly thing, especially when we're talking about this amount of money.

It is always, always better to wait for the right deal you feel good about rather than feel like you have to buy something now simply because stock is hard to come by. It'll keep! GTA 6 will still be there, I promise.

I'd hoped that Walmart and Best Buy would get their collective deal together at some point this Black Friday to actually provide meaningful deals on some flavor of PS5, PS5 Slim, or PS5 Pro, but that appears to continue to just be wishful thinking.

A quick look through both seems to indicate they are still flooded with bad, inflated deals with third-party marketplace sellers. In some cases, it would appear to even be the same marketplace vendor. For now, continue to avoid these bad deals, but it's worth keeping tabs on in case something changes.

One aspect of the whole "which version of the PS5 should I get" debate that often seems lacking is that, if you get a version of, say, the PS5 Slim or PS5 Pro that's only digital, you can always pick up a disc drive attachment later. It's not going to solve the problem of finding the exact console you want, but maybe it'll open up addition opens if you're really looking for one with a disc drive only.

PS5 disc drive for Digital Edition consoles | $79 at PS Direct

With another hour gone, what's the status for PS5 and PS5 Pro stock looking like? Well, friend, it's looking... worse than it was.

PS Direct still has the one option going for the refurbished PS5 Slim with disc drive, but GameStop appears to be out of the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro at the moment with only used and refurbished listings for the regular PS5. UK stock is basically still just that one EE bundle, but it has been holding on since we first caught wind of it earlier. Everywhere else is either wildly inflated or sold out.

Is it worth buying a PS5? Inevitably, this is the question I field most often from folks that don't eat, sleep, and breathe gaming. Makes sense; it's my job, and the expectation is that I would know.

I've said some version of this previously, but basically, if you're asking the question, you probably already have your mind made up. Nobody is dropping a grand or more without being fully committed to the purchase. But if you're truly on the fence, the best answer I've been able to come up with is: if you want to play games that look and play great without investing even more money into a gaming PC, this is your best option.

You can argument about console exclusives and so on until you're blue in the face, but at the end of the day, the PS5 Pro is cheaper than a good PC.

Speaking of inflated resellers, there's not much more than that over at Amazon for the time being when it comes to PS5 consoles, PS5 Pro or otherwise. Similar to other huge retailers, it's a good idea to check back in from time to time, but I'm here to tell you: you don't got to worry about it right now because there's nothing.

Spending all day trying to chase down a PS5 Pro, there's every chance you might at some point wonder, "Should I just hit up, I don't know, eBay or something?" The answer, resoundingly, is no, you absolutely should not.

Even ignoring all of the problems inherent to any site that allows for third-party auctions or resale items, it's simply just... full of bad deals. There's no world I can imagine where it's worth dropping an extra $600 or more just to get your hands on a PS5 Pro right this very moment. The top listing for a 2TB PS5 Pro – with an MSRP, as a reminder, of $899 – over on eBay right now? $1,750. I think not.

In an effort to do my due diligence and check in on likely PS5 Pro retailers, I've hit up most of the big ones several times. Most likely to restock, you know? But just in case you were wondering if some of the less-frequented ones have sneakily added stock, I've got bad news for you: Game, the UK retailer, seemingly... doesn't even have a PS5 (console) listing at the moment, or at least not one I could find.

But who knows? Maybe that'll change. Maybe not.

Speaking of refurbished PS5s: while I'd seen two different versions for sale over at PS Direct earlier, it looks like we're down to just the one refurbished PS5 Slim with disc drive product listing at this point.

Everything else remains as it was, which is to say: we're still out here trying to find you a good deal, but unless you're in the UK and want to take up EE on its bundled offer you might be out of luck for now. And don't fall for the inflated listings at the likes of Walmart and Best Buy.

Sometimes I get asked what the big difference is between refurbished and new and whether refurbished is still worth it when it comes to the PS5 and the short version is: depends on how much you trust PlayStation's recertification process, I guess.

"Every PlayStation certified refurbished product completes a rigorous recertification process that includes full testing that meets the same functional standards as new PlayStation products," PS Direct claims. "Your certified refurbished product works like new."

For me? I don't know. If I'm buying used, or refurbished, I'd hope for a bigger discount.

I find it's a good habit to periodically check back in with trusted retailers from time to time on big consoles like the PS5 Pro. Inevitably, it will drop big tech into the pool when you're least expecting it, and the only way to absolutely miss out is to not be paying attention.

That said, sometimes? Nothing changes. And for now, Best Buy remains completely empty on first-party PS5 Pro options. Bummer.

Rollin here, back at it again! Seems worth trying to answer: why is it so hard to get hold of the PS5 and PS5 Pro in general? The answer is... well, not exactly complicated, but it is multifaceted.

Shortest possible version? All technical hardware has had supply chain issues between parts and tariffs, making them overall more expensive. Then you have the simple fact that the PS5 Pro is, at current, the technical frontrunner for home consoles. You want the best place to play GTA 6 right now? It's on the PS5 Pro.

Add all of this to the usual holiday demand increase, and you get difficult-to-find PS5s, PS5 Slims, and PS5 Pros.

PS Direct's Certified Refurbished PS5 consoles are still firing away on the shelves and GameStop's PS5 Disc Edition is holding firm after the Digital Edition ran out of stock an hour ago.

Amazon, Walmart, and Newegg are still charging well over the odds for a PS5 as well, with no signs of a Pro console in sight.

Meanwhile in the UK, EE is still holding firm with that classic GTA 6 bundle, while PS Direct's supply of Digital Edition consoles is now debatable. My last check keeps turning up errors whenever I try and get on the digital version's page, so it looks like we might be out of luck here.

Amazon UK is estimating a February shipping date for its current PS5 stock, and that's for Prime members. Will it actually take that long, or is the retailer simply over-estimating while its warehouses run out of stock? That's difficult to tell for sure. After all, the store would be expected to receive more stock from Sony itself in that time.

I've seen this kind of movement before, and typically those delivery timings shrink down a little as stock refills warehouses after a period of increased demand. I wouldn't risk it while the PS5 remains available at other retailers, though.

The original PS5 pops back into circulation every now and then, usually via refurbished listings. However, GameStop has pre-owned consoles back in action today - at prices I wouldn't recommend touching. Asking $639.99 for the original device pre-owned when the Slim model is $549 certified refurbished from Sony is pretty ridiculous. Please don't take GameStop up on this offer, things aren't quite that desperate.

Tabs here, back for another hour of PS5 Pro restock hunting while Rollin grabs a bite to eat. I can see GameStop's PS5 Slim stock is starting to wane, so I'll check in there and see if there's any movement. Other than that, let's get a check on the market right now.

That EE GTA 6 bundle appears to still be going strong if you happen to be in the UK. While technically more expensive than just the console, it works out to a deal with the bundle controller and game. And let's be honest here: if you're looking to buy a PS5 Slim or PS5 Pro right now, there's a good chance it's because of GTA 6.

PS5 Digital Edition | GTA 6 | DualSense | £654.97 £605 at EE

That is the question! Ultimately, it is more expensive to get the version of the PS5 (Pro or Slim) with a disc drive. The value add is pretty obvious: either you can or you can't play discs.

As previously noted, there's some argument about whether that's worth the price increase, but to be frank: for me, it's a dealbreaker. We might be on the cusp of an all-digital future, maybe, but for now there's plenty of reasons to keep the ability to play a disc. The price increase is largely negligible if you're already dropping the cash for the console; why not do it right?

When we checked in a couple of hours ago, GameStop had both the PS5 Slim and PS5 Slim Digital Edition at MSRP, but it looks like maybe all good things must end as the digital version is seemingly no longer available. For now, the slightly more expensive version with a disc drive remains available, but who knows for how long.

Friends, I won't lie: PS5 Pro stock status is pretty bleak out there across both the US and UK. What listings there are, that I can find, have been wildly inflated by third-party sellers trying to take advantage of the situation.

GameStop and PS Direct still have some PS5 Slim stock, but PS Direct still appears to be refurbished while GameStop listing is... new, actually. How the turns table! In the UK, the EE bundle we've previously mentioned is still going – but who knows for how long.

While there are technically product listings for various PS5 consoles over at Newegg, they are similarly heavily inflated in the same way that Walmart's prices are inflated. Third-party sellers are the bane of my personal existence, but they're particularly gnarly in this specific scenario.

If you balk at MSRP, don't even think about dipping into these even pricier waters. While PS5s might be hard to come by, they're still being made (for now) and there will be another chance to not get gouged.

There's some question still as to whether the $899 is worth is for the PS5 Pro in 2026. Some on our team argue that there's really nothing in the Pro that makes it so significantly better as to justify the price; it's only worth it to those looking to get the absolute best experience.

I, however, would argue that the value here is that it's the best console on the market in a market that seems to be entirely ditching discs. If that matters to you (and it does to me) and you believe the writing to be on the wall for disc-based consoles then this might be your last, best option for a very long time. Worth getting in now before the price is even higher!

Best Buy previously had PS5 consoles on the shelves with slightly discounted copies of Wolverine. Alongside the rest of Best Buy's PS5 stock, though, they've since sold out. It's worth keeping an eye out here, though, it's been a few days since we've seen Sony's console on these shores.

Very has PS5 Slim consoles in stock and ready to go this morning, but it looks like they've been wiped out. The console was up and available as part of larger bundle deals, but you'll now simply find a PlayStation 5 listing page when you try the same link.

PS5 Pro stock still remains out of reach in both the US and the UK, though one Amazon listing in the former region is giving us reason for hope this morning.

The PS5 Slim is a little easier to find on the shelves - GameStop has both the Disc and Digital versions up for their regular MSRPs while PS Direct still has Certified Refurbished devices at a discount.

Across the pond, the UK is seeing of its better PS5 bundles right now, with EE offering up a PS5 Digital Edition alongside GTA 6 and a spare controller for nearly £50 off.

Walmart allows third party marketplace sellers onto its site, which often wreaks havoc on hard-to-find gadgets. That's happening with both PS5 and PS5 Pro stock this week. You'll find inflated prices in the four figures here right now - but they're not worth sacrificing cash for. Both consoles will be readily available in due time.

Amazon has the PS5 Pro bundled in with a few accessories as separate listings on its store right now. They're all out of stock at the moment, but it looks like there's been activity here recently. Jumping on and off the shelves in smaller releases, the PS5 Pro has been up for grabs here within the last day.

I've seen this from Amazon before. The site sometimes likes to release stock of hard-to-find gadgets in small pockets, frequently throughout the day. Keep that refresh button warm this weekend.

GameStop has both the PS5 Slim and PS5 Slim Digital Edition on the shelves for their regular MSRPs right now, which is a rare treat in itself at the moment. However, you can also grab 10% off a selection of pre-owned accessories at the same time. Separately, the site is also running discounts of up to $40 across PS5 games to boot.

I'm seeing EE's GTA 6 bundle everywhere at the moment, so it's likely moving fast at the retailer. The Digital Edition PS5 is at its regular rate here, with discounts on the game itself and that extra DualSense controller. Considering we're unlikely to see further savings on the console itself this year this is one of the better offers we've seen in some time.

PS5 Digital Edition | GTA 6 | DualSense | £654.97 £605 at EE

There's no need to spend over the odds for PS5 Pro stock if you're coming up short in regular hunts. The console is still difficult to get hold of, but drops have been spotted in the last few days. As an example, this Certified Refurbished device was up for $849 at PS Direct yesterday.

It's been run off the shelves now, but it's still well worth staying optimistic rather than paying reseller fees.
